name: 2 Corinthians
subtitle: A Ministry Made of Scripture
howToRead: Paul’s most personal letter is a defense of his ministry, and he defends it from Scripture. Its center is a reading of the Exodus: Moses veiled his face when the glory faded, but the ministers of the new covenant are unveiled, transformed from glory to glory — the old covenant written on stone against the new written by the Spirit on hearts of flesh. Around that argument the letter gathers the language of the prophets and psalms: the day of salvation now come, the cheerful giver, the treasure carried in clay jars, reconciliation, the new creation in which the old has passed away, and a thorn answered by grace made perfect in weakness. The chips beside each passage name the Scripture underneath it — solid for a formal quotation, dashed for an allusion, dotted for a fainter echo, ◇ for a figural pattern that borrows no words. A lighter chip and a trailing ? mark an echo that is faint or contested. Where Paul follows the Greek of the Septuagint against the Hebrew, both readings are shown.

pericopes.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the assembly of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The epistolary salutation 'Grace to you and peace' conjoins gift and shalom in a way that echoes the Aaronic blessing, where YHWH's gracious face and the gift of peace are invoked over Israel. The pairing of favor and peace as a divine bestowal is the priestly benediction's structure, and Paul speaks as one mediating God's blessing to the assembly. Volume is low and the wording is Paul's own formula, so this is a faint liturgical echo rather than a citation.

echoes.text: Yahweh will give strength to his people. Yahweh will bless his people with peace.
echoes.note: Paul's wish of 'peace from God' to the gathered saints resonates with the psalm's close, where YHWH gives strength and blesses his people with peace. The thematic coherence is the divine grant of peace to the covenant assembly. The echo is faint and competes with the broader Greco-Roman/Jewish letter convention, hence contested.

pericopes.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort; who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God. For as the sufferings of Christ abound to us, even so our comfort also abounds through Christ. But if we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which produces in you the patient enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer. Our hope for you is steadfast, knowing that, since you are partakers of the sufferings, so also are you of the comfort.

echoes.text: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
echoes.note: The titulature 'God of all comfort' who 'comforts us in all our affliction' draws directly on the programmatic 'Comfort, comfort my people' that opens Second Isaiah. The verbal density of comfort-language (parakaleo/paraklēsis) matches Isaiah's nacham/LXX parakaleite, and the consolation of an afflicted people awaiting redemption is the precise thematic field Paul occupies. High volume and recurrence across Isaiah make this the controlling text.

echoes.text: Sing, heavens; and be joyful, earth; and break out into singing, mountains: for Yahweh has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his afflicted.
echoes.note: Isaiah declares that YHWH 'has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted,' coupling consolation with mercy toward the afflicted exactly as Paul's 'Father of mercies and God of all comfort who comforts us in all our affliction.' The mercy/comfort/affliction triad is distinctive of the Servant-era consolation oracles, satisfying volume and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: For Yahweh has comforted Zion; he has comforted all her waste places, and has made her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of Yahweh; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody.
echoes.note: Isaiah promises that YHWH 'will comfort Zion, will comfort all her waste places,' a refrain of repeated comfort that Paul's piled-up paraklēsis vocabulary mirrors. The pattern of God comforting the desolate so they overflow with gladness coheres with Paul's logic that comfort received is comfort passed on. Recurrence of the comfort motif across Isaiah 51 strengthens availability.

echoes.text: “I, even I, am he who comforts you: who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die, and of the son of man who shall be made as grass;
echoes.note: 'I, even I, am he who comforts you' identifies God himself as the comforter of the afflicted and fearful, which is exactly Paul's confession that we 'are comforted by God.' The emphatic self-identification of God as comforter undergirds the title 'God of all comfort.' Strong thematic coherence and verbal overlap.

echoes.text: As one whom his mother comforts, so will I comfort you; and you will be comforted in Jerusalem.”
echoes.note: 'As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem' supplies the maternal-divine consolation image that Paul universalizes as the 'God of all comfort.' The promise that the comforted will themselves be settled and consoled coheres with Paul's chain of comfort flowing through sufferers to others. High volume of the comfort motif.

echoes.text: Break out into joy, sing together, you waste places of Jerusalem; for Yahweh has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'Break forth into joy... for YHWH has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem' ties comfort to redemption and corporate joy, paralleling Paul's link between shared suffering and shared comfort/salvation. The recurrence of the comfort-redemption pairing in Second Isaiah supports availability, though the verbal contact is lighter than 49:13 or 51:12.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The shepherd-God who gathers and gently carries the flock extends the consolation oracle's pastoral tenderness that 'Father of mercies' evokes. The echo is thematic rather than verbal and is subsidiary to the louder 40:1 contact.

echoes.text: In the multitude of my thoughts within me, your comforts delight my soul.
echoes.note: 'When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul' offers the closest psalmic parallel to comfort multiplying amid affliction, matching Paul's claim that as sufferings abound so comfort abounds. The psalm's vocabulary of divine consolation (LXX paraklēseis) gives verbal as well as thematic contact.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
echoes.note: 'YHWH is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit' coheres with Paul's God who draws near to comfort the afflicted. The psalm belongs to the deliverance-of-the-righteous-sufferer tradition Paul inhabits across the pericope, satisfying thematic coherence though the wording is comfort-adjacent rather than identical.

echoes.text: This is my comfort in my affliction, for your word has revived me.
echoes.note: 'This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life' fuses comfort, affliction, and life-giving promise in one verse, the same cluster Paul develops here and into 1:9-10. The shared comfort-in-affliction formula gives reasonable volume; the psalm's consolation idiom was readily available in Greek.

echoes.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
echoes.note: 'Your rod and your staff, they comfort me' provides the archetypal image of divine comfort in the midst of mortal danger, resonating with Paul's comfort amid sufferings. Volume is low and the contact is conceptual, so it is a faint supporting echo.

echoes.text: Her filthiness was in her skirts; she didn’t remember her latter end; therefore is she come down wonderfully; she has no comforter: see, Yahweh, my affliction; for the enemy has magnified himself.
echoes.note: Zion's lament 'there is none to comfort her' frames the absence Paul's 'God of all comfort' answers; the consolation oracles of Isaiah respond to exactly this Lamentations cry. The echo works intertextually with Isaiah rather than directly, hence low confidence and contested.

echoes.text: My son, if you come to serve the Lord, Prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, And make not haste in time of calamity. Cleave to him, and depart not, That you may be increased at your latter end. Accept whatever is brought upon you, And be longsuffering when you passest into humiliation. For gold is tried in the fire, And acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation. Put your trust in him, and he will help you: […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira's counsel that the one who would serve God should prepare for testing and endure affliction, trusting that God will help, parallels Paul's pairing of sufferings with steadfast hope and patient endurance. As a Second-Temple wisdom text it meets availability and offers thematic coherence on suffering-then-comfort, though no verbal quotation.

pericopes.text: For we don’t desire to have you uninformed, brothers, concerning our affliction which happened to us in Asia, that we were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so much that we despaired even of life. Yes, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead, who delivered us out of so great a death, and does deliver; on whom we have set our hope that he will also still deliver us; you also helping together on our behalf by your supplication; that, for the gift bestowed on us by means of many, thanks may be given by many persons on your behalf.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: Paul's confession of trust in 'God who raises the dead' draws on the canonical resurrection hope, of which Isaiah 26:19 ('your dead shall live, the dwellers in the dust shall awake') is a foundational text. Having received 'the sentence of death,' Paul grounds rescue in the God whose signature act is raising the dead, a distinctively Jewish-apocalyptic confession. Strong thematic coherence with the resurrection tradition.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The hope in the God 'who raises the dead' rests on the explicit resurrection promise that 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake.' Daniel is the clearest OT articulation of bodily resurrection and was central to Second-Temple resurrection faith, making it readily available as the conceptual source for Paul's title. High availability and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: to deliver their soul from death, to keep them alive in famine.
echoes.note: 'To deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine' matches Paul's 'delivered us out of so great a death, and does deliver,' the same verb-cluster of rescue from death. The psalm's confidence that God delivers from death rather than human strength parallels Paul's refusal to 'trust in ourselves.' Reasonable verbal and thematic contact.

echoes.text: For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.
echoes.note: 'You have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling' is a thanksgiving for rescue from mortal peril that closely tracks Paul's deliverance 'out of so great a death.' Psalm 116 is a deliverance-thanksgiving in which the rescued one calls on God and pays vows publicly, paralleling Paul's expectation of corporate thanksgiving (v. 11). Good thematic coherence.

echoes.text: The cords of death surrounded me. The floods of ungodliness made me afraid. The cords of Sheol were around me. The snares of death came on me. In my distress I called on Yahweh, and cried to my God. He heard my voice out of his temple. My cry before him came into his ears.
echoes.note: 'The cords of death encompassed me... in my distress I called upon YHWH... and he heard' supplies the deliverance-from-death-through-prayer pattern Paul reproduces: mortal peril, reliance on God, rescue, and the role of supplication (v. 11). Recurrence of this lament-to-rescue schema across the Psalter supports availability.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have brought up my soul from Sheol. You have kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit.
echoes.note: 'O YHWH, you brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit' frames rescue from death as a near-resurrection, mirroring Paul's link between deliverance from 'so great a death' and the God who raises the dead. Thematic coherence with the rescue-as-resurrection motif is strong.

echoes.text: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
echoes.note: Hannah's confession that 'YHWH kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up' grounds Paul's title 'God who raises the dead' in Israel's earliest doxology of divine life-and-death sovereignty. The bringing-down-then-raising movement matches Paul's death-sentence-then-deliverance experience. Good thematic coherence.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal, and there is none that can deliver out of my hand' is the Song of Moses' claim of exclusive power over death and rescue, underwriting Paul's confidence in God's deliverance against self-reliance. The kill/make-alive + deliver vocabulary aligns closely. Reasonable volume.

echoes.text: He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword.
echoes.note: 'He will deliver you in six troubles... in famine he will redeem you from death' offers a wisdom statement of repeated divine rescue from death matching Paul's 'delivered... and does deliver... will still deliver.' The triple-tense reliance on future rescue gives thematic coherence, though verbal contact is modest.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from Yahweh. For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good comes, but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, a salt land and not inhabited. Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose trust Yahweh is.
echoes.note: The contrast between the cursed who 'trust in man' and the blessed who 'trust in YHWH' undergirds Paul's purpose 'that we should not trust in ourselves but in God.' The trust-not-in-self / trust-in-God antithesis is the conceptual spine here, though Paul does not cite Jeremiah's wording. Faint but coherent.

echoes.text: For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me. But you have saved us from our adversaries, and have shamed those who hate us.
echoes.note: 'I will not trust in my bow... but you have saved us from our foes' parallels Paul's renunciation of self-reliance in favor of the God who delivers. Thematic coherence with the not-in-self-but-in-God logic; low volume of verbal contact.

echoes.text: For you have authority over life and death, And you lead down to the gates of Hades, and lead up again.
echoes.note: 'You have power over life and death; you lead down to the gates of Hades and back again' is a Second-Temple statement of God's authority to rescue from death that closely parallels Paul's God who raises the dead and delivers. As deuterocanonical it meets availability and offers a near-resurrection idiom, though verbal contact with Paul is loose.

echoes.text: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.
echoes.note: The martyr's hope that 'the King of the universe will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life' is a Second-Temple confession of God raising the dead amid suffering unto death, the same resurrection faith Paul invokes when under a death sentence. Availability is strong in the martyrological milieu; the contact is conceptual, not verbal.

pericopes.text: For our boasting is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in holiness and sincerity of God, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God we behaved ourselves in the world, and more abundantly toward you. For we write no other things to you, than what you read or even acknowledge, and I hope you will acknowledge to the end; as also you acknowledged us in part, that we are your boasting, even as you also are ours, in the day of our Lord Jesus.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Paul's 'boasting' grounded not in 'fleshly wisdom' but in God echoes Jeremiah's oracle that one should not boast in wisdom or might but boast in knowing YHWH. The wisdom-versus-true-boasting antithesis is precisely Jeremiah's, and Paul elsewhere cites this very passage, raising availability. Good thematic coherence despite no full quotation here.

echoes.text: Don’t boast about tomorrow; for you don’t know what a day may bring. Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
echoes.note: The wisdom counsel against self-boasting ('let another praise you, not your own mouth') informs Paul's careful, conscience-tested form of boasting. The contact is the moral evaluation of boasting rather than verbal, so it remains a faint wisdom echo.

echoes.text: I hold fast to my righteousness, and will not let it go. My heart shall not reproach me so long as I live.
echoes.note: 'I hold fast my righteousness... my heart does not reproach me for any of my days' is the classic appeal to a clear conscience that matches Paul's boast in 'the testimony of our conscience' to integrity of conduct. Job's self-defense by an unaccusing heart provides the closest OT analogue to Paul's conscience-language. Reasonable thematic coherence.

echoes.text: Yahweh administers judgment to the peoples. Judge me, Yahweh, according to my righteousness, and to my integrity that is in me.
echoes.note: 'Judge me, O YHWH, according to my righteousness and the integrity that is in me' parallels Paul's confidence before God in his holiness and sincerity of conduct. The appeal to inward integrity as the basis for vindication is shared, though Paul does not quote the psalm. Faint echo.

echoes.text: Love righteousness, you that be judges of the earth, Think you of the Lord with a good mind, And in singleness of heart seek you him;
echoes.note: 'Love righteousness... think of the Lord in goodness and seek him in sincerity (haplotēs) of heart' shares Paul's distinctive pairing of 'holiness and sincerity of God.' The sincerity/single-heartedness vocabulary is at home in Hellenistic-Jewish wisdom, satisfying availability; the contact is lexical-thematic rather than a citation.

pericopes.text: In this confidence, I was determined to come first to you, that you might have a second benefit; and by you to pass into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and to be sent forward by you on my journey to Judea. When I therefore was thus determined, did I show fickleness? Or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be the “Yes, yes” and the “No, no?” But as God is faithful, our word toward you was not “Yes and no.” For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, by me, Silvanus, and Timothy, was not “Yes and no,” but in him is “Yes.” For however many are the promises of God, in him is the “Yes.” Therefore also through him is the “Amen”, to the glory of God through us. Now he who establishes us with you in Christ, and anointed us, is God; who also sealed us, and gave us the down payment of the Spirit in our hearts.

echoes.text: so that he who blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he who swears in the earth shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hidden from my eyes.
echoes.note: Paul's claim that the promises find their 'Yes' and 'Amen' in Christ 'to the glory of God' draws on Isaiah's 'God of Amen/truth,' where one blesses and swears by the God of truth (LXX/Heb 'God of Amen'). The unusual liturgical 'Amen' tied to God's reliability points to this text as the lexical source for divine faithfulness sealing the promises. High thematic coherence with God's truthfulness.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: 'Know that YHWH your God is the faithful God who keeps covenant' grounds Paul's 'as God is faithful' and the certainty that all God's promises are confirmed (Yes/Amen). The covenant-keeping faithfulness of God is the theological basis for Paul's argument that his word, mirroring God's, is not equivocating Yes-and-No. Good thematic coherence.

echoes.text: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor the son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken, and will he not make it good?
echoes.note: 'God is not a man that he should lie... has he said, and will he not do it?' directly supports Paul's contrast between human fickleness and God's reliable Yes to his promises. The denial of divine vacillation undergirds the Yes/Amen argument. Reasonable verbal-thematic contact on God keeping his word.

echoes.text: Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brothers: and the Spirit of Yahweh came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up, and went to Ramah.
echoes.note: Paul's 'he... anointed us' draws on the anointing tradition in which Samuel anoints David and 'the Spirit of YHWH came mightily upon him.' The conjunction of anointing with the gift of the Spirit (v. 22) maps onto this royal-prophetic anointing pattern. Good thematic coherence between anointing and Spirit-endowment.

echoes.text: You shall make it a holy anointing oil, a perfume compounded after the art of the perfumer: it shall be a holy anointing oil. You shall use it to anoint the Tent of Meeting, the ark of the testimony, the table and all its articles, the lamp stand and its accessories, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin with its base. You shall sanctify them, that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them shall be holy. […]
echoes.note: The holy anointing oil that consecrates priests and the tent supplies the consecration imagery behind 'he... anointed us... and gave us the Spirit.' Anointing as a setting-apart for God's service coheres with Paul's claim that God establishes, anoints, and seals believers. Availability is strong though the application is figural.

echoes.text: In that day, says Yahweh of Armies, will I take you, Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel,’ says Yahweh, ‘and will make you as a signet, for I have chosen you,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”
echoes.note: 'I will make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you' offers the OT 'seal' image of God designating and securing his chosen one, behind Paul's 'who also sealed us.' The signet/seal as a mark of ownership and guaranteed status matches Paul's sealing tied to the Spirit-down-payment. Reasonable thematic coherence.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' is the eschatological Spirit-gift that Paul claims as already given 'in our hearts' as a down payment. The lavish outpouring of the Spirit on God's people in the last days underwrites Paul's arrabon language. Good availability and thematic coherence with Spirit-as-pledge.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you' supplies the promise of the indwelling Spirit that Paul says God 'gave... in our hearts.' The new-covenant gift of an internal Spirit, paired with a new heart, coheres precisely with Paul's sealing and down-payment of the Spirit in the heart. Strong thematic coherence.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: 'I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts' provides the new-covenant interiorization motif behind Paul's Spirit given 'in our hearts' as guarantee. The heart as the locus of God's confirming work coheres with Paul's establishing/sealing language. Recurrence with Ezekiel 36 strengthens the new-covenant background.

echoes.text: He said, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know that I will inherit it?” He said to him, “Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon.” He brought him all of these, and divided them in the middle, and laid each half opposite the other; but he didn’t divide the birds. The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them away. When the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on […]
echoes.note: The covenant in which God guarantees his promise to Abraham models the down-payment/pledge logic that the promises are sure and confirmed (Yes/Amen). The arrabon as a first installment securing the whole resonates with God's covenant guarantee. Conceptual rather than verbal, hence low.

echoes.text: He has remembered his covenant forever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations, the covenant which he made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac, and confirmed the same to Jacob for a statute; to Israel for an everlasting covenant,
echoes.note: 'He remembers his covenant forever... which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute' restates the reliability of God's promises that Paul affirms as Yes in Christ. The motif of God establishing/confirming his promise to many generations parallels 'establishes us... in Christ.' Faint thematic echo.

echoes.text: He said, “I will send you a young goat from the flock.” She said, “Will you give me a pledge, until you send it?” He said, “What pledge will I give you?” She said, “Your signet and your cord, and your staff that is in your hand.” He gave them to her, and came in to her, and she conceived by him.
echoes.note: The pledge (Heb erabon, the Semitic source of Greek arrabon) Judah leaves with Tamar is the lexical background for Paul's 'down payment of the Spirit.' The shared erabon/arrabon term marks the Spirit as a deposit guaranteeing full payment to come. Contact is lexical-etymological, so low confidence and contested.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The Spirit of YHWH shall rest upon him' (the anointed messianic shoot) extends the anointing-with-Spirit pattern that Paul applies to believers in Christ ('anointed us... gave us the Spirit'). The messianic anointing background coheres figurally; verbal contact with Paul is light.

echoes.text: I will not break my covenant, nor alter what my lips have uttered. Once have I sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David. His seed will endure forever, his throne like the sun before me. It will be established forever like the moon, the faithful witness in the sky.” Selah.
echoes.note: 'I will not violate my covenant or alter the word that went forth from my lips... his line shall endure forever' affirms God's unalterable, faithful word that Paul echoes in 'God is faithful, our word was not Yes and No.' The non-vacillation of the divine promise coheres with Paul's argument. Faint echo.

pericopes.text: But I call God for a witness to my soul, that I didn’t come to Corinth to spare you. Not that we control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy. For you stand firm in faith.

echoes.text: Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven. He who vouches for me is on high.
echoes.note: Paul's solemn 'I call God for a witness to my soul' echoes Job's appeal, 'even now, behold, my witness is in heaven,' invoking God as the guarantor of one's truthfulness. The recourse to God-as-witness in self-defense against suspicion is the shared rhetorical move. Reasonable thematic coherence with the heavenly-witness motif.

echoes.text: He said to them, “Yahweh is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand.” They said, “He is witness.”
echoes.note: Samuel's 'YHWH is witness against you... that you have found nothing in my hand' is a formal oath calling God to attest the speaker's integrity, paralleling Paul's calling God as witness to his motives. The covenant-lawsuit form of invoking God as witness is well attested and available. Good thematic coherence.

echoes.text: If you afflict my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, no man is with us; behold, God is witness between me and you.”
echoes.note: 'God is witness between you and me' in the Laban-Jacob covenant supplies the oath-formula of summoning God to witness sincerity of intent, the same form Paul uses. The contact is to the conventional witness-oath rather than to specific wording, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: You shall fear Yahweh your God; and you shall serve him, and shall swear by his name.
echoes.note: The command to fear God and 'swear by his name' frames the legitimacy of calling God to witness an oath, which Paul does regarding his change of travel plans. The contact is to the sanctioned practice of God-invoking oaths rather than to the verse's wording. Faint echo.

echoes.text: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant.
echoes.note: 'YHWH was witness between you' uses the same God-as-witness formula Paul employs to attest the truth of his conduct toward the Corinthians. The prophetic deployment of the witness-oath shows the idiom's availability; verbal contact with Paul is conventional. Low confidence.

pericopes.text: But I determined this for myself, that I would not come to you again in sorrow. For if I make you sorry, then who will make me glad but he who is made sorry by me? And I wrote this very thing to you, so that, when I came, I wouldn’t have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy would be shared by all of you. For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not that you should be made sorry, but that you might know the love that I have so abundantly for you.

echoes.text: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a spring of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
echoes.note: Paul writes 'with many tears' out of 'much affliction and anguish of heart,' grieving over a community he loves. Jeremiah's wish that his head were waters to weep day and night for his people supplies the prophetic prototype of the leader who weeps over those under his charge. Coherence is strong (Paul's self-presentation as a suffering apostle); volume is low since there is no shared diction.

echoes.text: I am weary with my groaning. Every night I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears.
echoes.note: 'I wrote to you with many tears' resonates with the lament psalmist who floods his bed with weeping. The motif of tears poured out in anguish of heart is a stock Psalter idiom Paul would have internalized. Faint and diffuse, marked low for lack of verbal anchor.

echoes.text: The troubles of my heart are enlarged. Oh bring me out of my distresses.
echoes.note: 'Anguish of heart' (v.4) matches the psalmist's 'the troubles of my heart are enlarged.' The Greek thlipsis/synochē kardias language draws on LXX heart-distress vocabulary. Volume is low; recorded as an available Septuagintal coloring of Paul's affliction language.

pericopes.text: But if any has caused sorrow, he has caused sorrow, not to me, but in part (that I not press too heavily) to you all. Sufficient to such a one is this punishment which was inflicted by the many; so that on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him. For to this end I also wrote, that I might know the proof of you, whether you are obedient in all things. Now I also forgive whomever you forgive anything. For if indeed I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven that one for your sakes in the presence of Christ, that no advantage may be gained over us by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his schemes.

echoes.text: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
echoes.note: Paul urges the church to 'forgive him and comfort (parakaleō) him' lest he be overwhelmed. The comfort/paraklēsis vocabulary that saturates 2 Corinthians is rooted in Isaiah 40's 'Comfort, comfort my people,' the LXX charter text for eschatological consolation. Coherence with the letter's comfort theme is high; verbal echo is real but generic, hence medium.

echoes.text: Don’t let the flood waters overwhelm me, neither let the deep swallow me up. Don’t let the pit shut its mouth on me.
echoes.note: The offender risks being 'swallowed up' (katapinō) by excessive sorrow. The lament psalmist prays not to be swallowed by the flood or have the pit close its mouth over him; the verb katapinō is the LXX term for being engulfed/overwhelmed. Volume is moderate through the shared swallowing imagery applied to a person drowning in grief.

echoes.text: The Lord has become as an enemy, he has swallowed up Israel; He has swallowed up all her palaces, he has destroyed his strongholds; He has multiplied in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.
echoes.note: 'Swallowed up' (katepothē) is the repeated verb of Lamentations for the Lord engulfing Zion in sorrow. Paul fears the penitent will be similarly engulfed by grief. The figural link is to overwhelming communal sorrow; low because the LXX term is common and the referent differs.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: Paul guards against 'Satan' gaining advantage, 'for we are not ignorant of his schemes.' The figure of ha-satan operating against the faithful, testing and seeking advantage before God, is established in the Job prologue (and Job 2:1-7). Availability and coherence are strong: Satan as the adversarial accuser is a Second-Temple development of this OT scene.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: Satan's 'schemes' to gain advantage echo the satan standing at God's right hand to accuse Joshua the high priest, only to be rebuked. The accuser seeking legal advantage over God's people informs Paul's worry about being outwitted. Medium: thematically apt accuser imagery without verbal overlap.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”
echoes.note: 'We are not ignorant of his schemes (noēmata)' recalls the serpent who was 'more crafty/subtle' than any beast, the archetypal deceiver of God's people. Paul elsewhere (2 Cor 11:3) makes this Eden-craftiness link explicit, raising the recurrence weight here. The scheming-deceiver coherence is strong; verbal volume low.

echoes.text: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.
echoes.note: Satan 'incited' David to a course that brought ruin, a parade case of the adversary gaining advantage over a leader. Paul's anxiety not to give Satan an opening fits this pattern. Low confidence: thematic only, one of several OT satan-scenes available.

pericopes.text: Now when I came to Troas for the Good News of Christ, and when a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no relief for my spirit, because I didn’t find Titus, my brother, but taking my leave of them, I went out into Macedonia.

echoes.text: Among these nations you will find no ease, and there will be no rest for the sole of your foot; but Yahweh will give you there a trembling heart, failing of eyes, and pining of soul.
echoes.note: 'I had no relief for my spirit' (ouk eschēka anesin tō pneumati) echoes the covenant-curse condition of finding 'no rest for the sole of your foot' and an 'anxious/trembling heart.' Paul's restlessness over Titus is colored by this LXX no-rest idiom. Low: diffuse mood-echo, no quotation.

echoes.text: I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'A door was opened to me in the Lord' may resonate with Hosea's 'door of hope' (petach tiqvah) opened in the wilderness as a gateway to renewed mission. The image of a divinely opened door of opportunity is faint and contested, as the Roman idiom of an 'open door' for preaching may be independent. Marked low.

pericopes.text: Now thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and reveals through us the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place. For we are a sweet aroma of Christ to God, in those who are saved, and in those who perish; to the one a stench from death to death; to the other a sweet aroma from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things? For we are not as so many, peddling the word of God. But as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God, we speak in Christ.

echoes.text: but its innards and its legs he shall wash with water. The priest shall burn all of it on the altar, for a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The sweet aroma (osmē euōdias)' Paul and his ministry spread is the exact LXX sacrificial formula for the burnt offering: 'an offering by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.' Paul casts apostolic ministry as a sacrifice whose fragrance ascends. Volume is high on the set phrase osmē euōdias; medium overall because the phrase recurs across the whole sacrificial system rather than one verse.

echoes.text: Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma. Yahweh said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I ever again strike every living thing, as I have done.
echoes.note: The first 'pleasing aroma' (osmē euōdias) is Noah's offering, which God 'smelled' and was reconciled. Paul's fragrance imagery for a ministry that mediates reconciliation draws on this foundational pleasing-odor scene. Medium: shares the precise LXX formula but is one instance among several aroma texts.

echoes.text: You shall burn the whole ram on the altar: it is a burnt offering to Yahweh; it is a pleasant aroma, an offering made by fire to Yahweh.
echoes.note: The ordination ram offered as 'a pleasing aroma, an offering by fire to the LORD' supplies priestly-consecration coloring to Paul's self-presentation as a fragrant offering in service of God. The ordination context coheres with Paul's apostolic vocation. Medium on shared formula.

echoes.text: As a pleasant aroma will I accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples, and gather you out of the countries in which you have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you in the sight of the nations.
echoes.note: 'As a pleasing aroma I will accept you when I bring you out from the peoples' applies the sacrificial-fragrance formula to God's restored people gathered from the nations. Paul, spreading the aroma 'in every place' among saved and perishing, picks up this universalized, gathering sense of the pleasing odor. Medium.

echoes.text: For from the rising of the sun even to the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering: for my name is great among the nations,” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'In every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations.' Paul's aroma of the knowledge of God spread 'in every place' strikingly combines fragrant offering + worldwide diffusion among the nations, matching Malachi's vision. Coherence with Paul's Gentile mission is high; medium for the inexact wording.

echoes.text: As cinnamon and aspalathus, I have given a scent of perfumes; And as choice myrrh, I spread abroad a pleasant odour; As galbanum, and onyx, and stacte, And as the fume of frankincense in the tabernacle.
echoes.note: Personified Wisdom says she gave forth fragrance 'like cinnamon and aromatic balm... like choice myrrh... like the fragrance of incense in the tabernacle,' spreading her aroma. Paul's 'fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place' transposes Wisdom's self-diffusing aroma onto the knowledge of God in Christ. Strong thematic coherence (fragrance = diffused divine knowledge); medium for deuterocanonical, non-verbal link.

echoes.text: Your oils have a pleasing fragrance. Your name is oil poured out, therefore the virgins love you.
echoes.note: 'Your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out, therefore the maidens love you' offers the erotic-devotional register of a fragrant, beloved name. Paul's aroma of Christ that draws (or repels) may glance at this beloved-name fragrance. Low: evocative but lacks verbal contact and the sacrificial frame dominates.

echoes.text: They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh, as the waters cover the sea.
echoes.note: Paul spreads 'the knowledge of him in every place,' which resonates with the eschatological promise that 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD.' The universal diffusion of divine knowledge is the shared note. Low/medium: thematic, mediated through the aroma metaphor.

echoes.text: You have ascended on high. You have led away captives. You have received gifts among men, yes, among the rebellious also, that Yah God might dwell there.
echoes.note: 'God always leads us in triumph (thriambeuō)' uses the Roman triumphal-procession image, but its OT analogue is the divine warrior who 'ascended on high, leading captives in your train.' Paul figures himself among those led in God's victory train. Low: the primary background is Greco-Roman, not OT, so this is a faint figural overlay.

echoes.text: Moses said to Yahweh, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”
echoes.note: 'Who is sufficient for these things?' echoes Moses' protest of inadequacy at his call ('I am not eloquent... I am slow of speech'), the paradigm of human insufficiency for a divine commission answered by God's enabling. Paul's rhetorical question and his later 'our sufficiency is from God' (3:5) make the call-narrative resonance coherent. Medium.

echoes.text: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?
echoes.note: 'Who is sufficient/who can endure it?' (tis estai hikanos / tis hypoisei) matches the prophetic exclamation before the overwhelming Day of the LORD. Paul's 'who is sufficient (hikanos) for these things?' may pick up this LXX idiom of human inadequacy before God's awesome work. Low: shared rhetorical form, divergent context.

echoes.text: Your silver has become dross, your wine mixed with water.
echoes.note: Paul condemns those 'peddling (kapēleuō) the word of God,' the verb for a huckster/tavern-keeper who adulterates wares. Isaiah's indictment 'your wine is mixed with water' (LXX: tavern-keepers diluting wine) is the prophetic image of corrupting/cheapening what is holy for profit. Coherence with Paul's charge of adulterating God's word is good; low because the link is conceptual, not quoted.

pericopes.text: Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, as do some, letters of commendation to you or from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men; being revealed that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain, and stay here, and I will give you the stone tablets with the law and the commands that I have written, that you may teach them.”
echoes.note: The contrast 'not on tablets of stone' deliberately evokes the stone tablets God gave Moses, which Exodus 24:12 first announces ('the tables of stone, and the law, and the commandment, which I have written'). Volume is high (verbal 'tablets of stone') and the whole chapter is a sustained reading of the Sinai narrative, satisfying coherence and availability.

echoes.text: He gave to Moses, when he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.
echoes.note: Paul's 'tablets of stone written... with the Spirit of the living God' inverts Exodus 31:18, where the two tables of testimony were 'tables of stone, written with the finger of God.' The Spirit/finger-of-God substitution is a precise figural play, and the phrase 'tablets of stone' is near-quotation.

echoes.text: Moses turned, and went down from the mountain, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand; tablets that were written on both their sides; on the one side and on the other they were written. The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tables.
echoes.note: Exodus 32:15-16 stresses that the tables were 'written on both their sides' and that 'the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables.' Paul's antithesis of divine writing on stone versus writing by the Spirit on hearts draws on this stone-tablet imagery; slightly lower volume than 31:18 since the verbal anchor is shared across the cluster.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Chisel two stone tablets like the first: and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.
echoes.note: Exodus 34:1 ('Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first') supplies the renewed-covenant tablets that frame the very Exodus 34 narrative Paul exposits across the chapter. Coherence with the chapter's overall theme is strong, though the specific stone-tablet phrase is drawn from the whole cluster.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: 'Written... on tablets of human hearts' echoes Jeremiah 31:33, where God promises to 'put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.' Recurrence is strong: Paul names a 'new covenant' (3:6) directly from Jer 31:31, making the heart-inscription allusion here mutually reinforcing and high-confidence.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: 'Hearts of flesh' as the surface of inscription, contrasted with stone, directly takes up Ezekiel 36:26: 'I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.' The stone/flesh-heart antithesis is verbally exact and thematically central, scoring high on volume and coherence.

echoes.text: I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh;
echoes.note: Ezekiel 11:19 ('I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh') is the parallel oracle to 36:26 and joined to the gift of a 'new spirit,' which coheres with Paul's 'Spirit of the living God' writing on hearts of flesh. Recurrence across Ezekiel strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of your altars;
echoes.note: Jeremiah 17:1 says Judah's sin is 'graven... upon the table of their heart' with a pen of iron — the inverse image of God's good writing on hearts. Paul may echo this 'table of the heart' idiom; volume is modest and the valence is reversed, so it is faint and contested.

echoes.text: Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck. Write them on the tablet of your heart.
echoes.note: Proverbs 3:3 urges writing mercy and truth 'upon the table of thine heart,' a sapiential idiom for internalized teaching that Paul's heart-tablet language may draw on. The verbal overlap ('table of the heart') is real but the source is more plausibly the prophetic new-covenant texts, so this is a contested secondary echo.

echoes.text: Bind them on your fingers. Write them on the tablet of your heart.
echoes.note: Proverbs 7:3 ('write them upon the table of thine heart') repeats the same sapiential heart-tablet idiom and reinforces its availability in Paul's scriptural vocabulary. Faint and contested for the same reason as 3:3; listed for recurrence of the idiom.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke these words to all your assembly on the mountain out of the midst of the fire, of the cloud, and of the thick darkness, with a great voice. He added no more. He wrote them on two stone tablets, and gave them to me.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy 5:22 recalls the Decalogue 'written... in two tables of stone' delivered at Horeb, part of the broad stone-tablet tradition behind Paul's antithesis. Lower volume than the Exodus passages, so a faint corroborating echo.

pericopes.text: Such confidence we have through Christ toward God; not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God; who also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant; not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
echoes.note: 'Servants of a new covenant' (3:6) is a direct appropriation of Jeremiah 31:31, the only OT text to name a 'new covenant.' Volume and distinctiveness are very high, and it anchors the heart-writing allusions of 3:3 and the whole chapter's covenant theology.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant promise that the law would be inward 'Spirit not letter' depends on Jeremiah 31:33 ('I will write it in their hearts'). Recurrence with 3:3 and 3:6's covenant language makes this a coherent, high-confidence allusion to the same oracle.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: Paul's 'Spirit gives life' against the death-dealing 'letter' draws on Ezekiel 36:27, 'I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes' — the Spirit internalizing the law. This pairs with Jer 31 to ground the letter/Spirit antithesis and scores high on coherence.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'The Spirit gives life' echoes the valley-of-bones promise, Ezekiel 37:14: 'I shall put my spirit in you, and ye shall live.' The life-giving function of the Spirit is verbally and thematically tight, and Ezekiel's spirit-life motif coheres with Paul's new-covenant argument.

echoes.text: Thus says the Lord Yahweh to these bones: Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you shall live.
echoes.note: Ezekiel 37:5-6 ('I will cause breath/spirit to enter into you, and ye shall live') reinforces the Spirit-vivifies-the-dead imagery behind 'the Spirit gives life.' Recurrence within Ezekiel 37 strengthens the allusion cluster; slightly lower volume than v.14.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The life-giving Spirit/breath that animates dead matter may echo Genesis 2:7, where God breathes the breath of life and man becomes a living soul. Plausible figural backdrop to 'the Spirit gives life,' but volume is low and the Ezekiel new-covenant texts are the nearer source, so contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy 30:6 ('the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart... that thou mayest live') anticipates the inward, life-giving renewal Paul ascribes to the Spirit over against the letter. A faint coherence-driven echo to the heart-circumcision tradition behind new-covenant interiority.

pericopes.text: But if the service of death, written engraved on stones, came with glory, so that the children of Israel could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses for the glory of his face; which was passing away: won’t service of the Spirit be with much more glory? For if the service of condemnation has glory, the service of righteousness exceeds much more in glory. For most certainly that which has been made glorious has not been made glorious in this respect, by reason of the glory that surpasses. For if that which passes away was with glory, much more that which remains is in glory.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him. When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him.
echoes.note: 'The children of Israel could not look steadfastly on the face of Moses for the glory of his face' is a close paraphrase of Exodus 34:29-30, where Moses' face shone and Aaron and Israel 'were afraid to come nigh him.' This is the interpretive center of the whole pericope; volume and coherence are maximal.

echoes.text: The children of Israel saw Moses’ face, that the skin of Moses’ face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with him.
echoes.note: Exodus 34:35 ('the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face shone') supplies the shining-face datum Paul reads as a fading glory. Recurrence across 34:29-35 and verbal overlap ('face of Moses... shone/glory') make this a strong allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Chisel two stone tablets like the first: and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.
echoes.note: 'The service of death, written engraved on stones' identifies the Mosaic ministry with the stone tablets of the renewed covenant in Exodus 34:1. The 'engraved on stones' phrase links the glory of Moses' face specifically to the inscribed Decalogue, a figural reading of the Exodus 34 tablets.

echoes.text: He gave to Moses, when he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.
echoes.note: 'Written engraved on stones' recalls the tables 'written with the finger of God' (Exodus 31:18), the same tablets Paul names a 'ministry of death.' Reinforces the stone-tablet motif from 3:3; medium because the stone-tablet phrasing is shared across the Sinai cluster.

echoes.text: Yahweh delivered to me the two stone tablets written with the finger of God On them were all the words which Yahweh spoke with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire in the day of the assembly.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy 9:10 describes 'two tables of stone written with the finger of God' bearing the commandments — the engraved-on-stone law Paul calls the ministry of death/condemnation. A faint corroborating echo of the stone-engraving tradition.

pericopes.text: Having therefore such a hope, we use great boldness of speech, and not as Moses, who put a veil on his face, that the children of Israel wouldn’t look steadfastly on the end of that which was passing away. But their minds were hardened, for until this very day at the reading of the old covenant the same veil remains, because in Christ it passes away. But to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies on their heart.

echoes.text: When Moses was done speaking with them, he put a veil on his face.
echoes.note: 'Moses, who put a veil on his face' directly cites Exodus 34:33: 'till Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face.' The veil is the load-bearing image of Paul's argument; verbal volume and coherence are maximal.

echoes.text: The children of Israel saw Moses’ face, that the skin of Moses’ face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with him.
echoes.note: Exodus 34:35 ('Moses put the vail upon his face again, until he went in to speak with him') gives the repeated veiling Paul reinterprets as concealing the glory's end. Recurrence with 34:33 strengthens the allusion; Paul's 'reading of the old covenant' makes the Sinai veil a hermeneutical figure.

echoes.text: When Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come near him.
echoes.note: The Israelites' inability to gaze (v.13, 'wouldn't look steadfastly on the end of that which was passing away') recalls their fear before Moses' shining face in Exodus 34:30. Coherent continuation of the shining-face motif into the veil pericope.

echoes.text: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: 'Their minds were hardened' and a veil 'on their heart' resonate with Isaiah 6:10's hardening of heart so the people cannot perceive — a stock prophetic hardening motif Paul applies to Israel's reading of Moses. Faint and contested, since the immediate frame is the Exodus veil.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy 29:4 ('the LORD hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see... unto this day') parallels Paul's 'until this very day... a veil remains' and 'minds were hardened.' The 'unto this day' obduracy idiom is a plausible faint source; contested against the Exodus veil frame.

pericopes.text: But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.

echoes.text: But when Moses went in before Yahweh to speak with him, he took the veil off, until he came out; and he came out, and spoke to the children of Israel that which he was commanded.
echoes.note: 'Whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away' rewrites Exodus 34:34: 'when Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he took the vail off.' Paul transposes Moses' going-in-to-the-Lord into the believer's turning to the Lord; near-quotation with high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: The children of Israel saw Moses’ face, that the skin of Moses’ face shone: and Moses put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with him.
echoes.note: 'With unveiled face' (3:18) inverts Exodus 34:35, where Israel saw Moses re-veil his shining face; now all believers behold with face unveiled. The veil/unveiled antithesis depends directly on the Exodus 34 veiling scene.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.
echoes.note: 'Beholding/seeing the glory of the Lord... transformed into the same image from glory to glory' figurally generalizes Moses' transformation in Exodus 34:29, where his face shone from speaking with the LORD. Paul makes the Sinai theophany the pattern of Christian transfiguration; strong coherence with the chapter.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: 'Transformed into the same image' draws on the creation of humanity 'in the image of God' (Genesis 1:26-27); the glory once on Moses' face is being restored as the divine image in believers. A figural creation/new-creation reading; medium because 'image' could be primarily Christological.

echoes.text: For you have made him a little lower than God, and crowned him with glory and honor.
echoes.note: Psalm 8:5 ('crowned him with glory and honour') articulates humanity's glory, which Paul sees restored as believers go 'from glory to glory.' A faint thematic echo of the glory-of-the-image tradition; contested and low volume.

echoes.text: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?”
echoes.note: 'Seeing the glory of the Lord' uses the Exodus theophanic formula 'the glory of the LORD' (e.g., Exodus 16:7; 24:16-17; 40:34-35), the glory that settled on Sinai and the tabernacle. A faint availability echo of the wilderness glory tradition behind Paul's Sinai exposition.

echoes.text: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: 'As in a mirror' beholding glory and being transformed into the image may echo Wisdom 7:26, where Wisdom is 'the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness.' A Second-Temple availability echo linking mirror, image, and divine glory; faint and contested.

pericopes.text: Therefore seeing we have this ministry, even as we obtained mercy, we don’t faint. But we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’”
echoes.note: Paul's 'craftiness' (panourgia) echoes the LXX description of the serpent as panourgos in Genesis 3:1, a link he makes explicit at 2 Cor 11:3. Coherence is decent (Paul's recurring serpent/deception polemic) but volume here is faint, so the verbal contact is best treated as a thematic echo.

echoes.text: The thoughts of the righteous are just, but the advice of the wicked is deceitful.
echoes.note: 'Handling the word of God deceitfully' versus 'manifestation of the truth' replays the wisdom contrast between deceitful counsels and honest speech. The link is generic to the sapiential tradition rather than to a single verse, hence low volume.

pericopes.text: Even if our Good News is veiled, it is veiled in those who perish; in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, that the light of the Good News of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not dawn on them. For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake; seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

echoes.text: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: The 'god of this world has blinded the minds' so they cannot see the light recasts Isaiah's hardening commission, where eyes are made blind 'lest they see.' High recurrence in Paul (Rom 11:8) and strong coherence with the veiling theme of ch. 3 support a deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's lament that the LORD had 'not given a heart to know, eyes to see' supplies the unbelief-as-imposed-blindness motif Paul fuses with Isaiah. Paul cites this very verse in Rom 11:8, raising its availability and coherence here.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant's task to 'open blind eyes' frames Paul's gospel as the light that should dawn; 42:19's 'blind servant' sharpens the irony of unbelieving blindness. Volume is moderate but coherence with the Isaianic light/blindness cluster Paul is mining is strong.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
echoes.note: Calling Christ 'the image of God' reads the creation of humanity in God's image figurally, with Christ as the true eikon. The pairing of image (4:4) and the creation of light (4:6) keys the whole pericope to Genesis 1, making this a deliberate new-creation typology.

echoes.text: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom as 'image of his goodness' and radiance of glory is the Second-Temple lexicon for Christ as 'image of God' and 'glory of Christ.' Availability and coherence are high; volume rests on shared eikon/glory vocabulary rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: 'God who said, Light will shine out of darkness' rewords the creation fiat, presenting conversion as a new act of creation in the heart. The volume is high (clear verbal evocation of the fiat lux) and coherent with the Genesis 1 image motif of 4:4.

echoes.text: For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.
echoes.note: 'The light of the knowledge of the glory of God' closely tracks Habakkuk's promise that the earth will be filled with 'the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.' The triple chain knowledge-glory-LORD is distinctive enough to register as more than coincidence.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: Light shining on those in darkness echoes Isaiah's people who 'walked in darkness' seeing a great light, reinforcing the gospel-as-dawn imagery. Coherent with the Isaianic light theme already in play, though the verbal contact is general.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.
echoes.note: 'The glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ' continues ch. 3's contrast with the glory on Moses' face, transferring the shining-face motif to Christ. Recurrence from the immediately prior argument makes the Exodus glory narrative the controlling subtext.

pericopes.text: But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.

echoes.text: The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, How are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!
echoes.note: 'Precious sons of Zion' reckoned as 'earthen pots, the work of the potter' supplies the exact pairing of priceless worth held in cheap clay vessels that Paul exploits. The treasure/earthen-vessel antithesis gives this strong coherence and notable volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The 'clay vessel' housing divine power evokes the human creature formed from dust and animated by God's breath, so the frailty is constitutive of creaturehood. Figural rather than verbal, but it grounds Paul's 'not from ourselves' in the dust-origin of humanity.

echoes.text: But now, Yahweh, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you our potter; and we all are the work of your hand.
echoes.note: 'We are the clay, you our potter' establishes the creature-as-vessel theme that Paul presses to magnify God's power over human weakness. Availability and coherence are strong within Paul's potter/clay usage (Rom 9:21).

echoes.text: How much more, those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed before the moth!
echoes.note: Those who 'dwell in houses of clay' and are easily crushed parallel the fragility of the clay vessel motif. Volume is faint and the contact is conceptual, so it functions only as a supporting echo.

echoes.text: He divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put into the hands of all of them trumpets, and empty pitchers, with torches within the pitchers.
echoes.note: Gideon's torches hidden in clay jars, broken to flash God's deliverance, joins the light of 4:6 to the clay vessels of 4:7: divine power shines precisely when the fragile jar is shattered. The shared jar+light+power configuration gives this a striking coherence.

pericopes.text: We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed;

echoes.text: Yah has punished me severely, but he has not given me over to death.
echoes.note: 'Struck down, yet not destroyed' closely matches the psalmist's 'the LORD has chastened me severely, but has not given me over to death.' The structure of severe affliction stopped just short of destruction is the same, supplying good volume for the climactic clause.

echoes.text: Though he stumble, he shall not fall, for Yahweh holds him up with his hand.
echoes.note: 'Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down, for the LORD upholds his hand' mirrors the not-forsaken/not-destroyed paradox of the righteous sufferer. Coherent with Paul's hardship-catalog theology of divine sustenance.

echoes.text: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.”
echoes.note: 'Pursued, yet not forsaken' echoes the covenant assurance that God 'will not leave you nor forsake you.' The phrase is widespread, so volume is low and the link is a general scriptural commonplace.

pericopes.text: always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body. For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus may be revealed in our mortal flesh. So then death works in us, but life in you.

echoes.text: Yes, for your sake we are killed all day long. We are regarded as sheep for the slaughter.
echoes.note: 'Always delivered to death for Jesus' sake' anticipates the very verse ('we are killed all day long') Paul quotes at Rom 8:36, casting apostolic suffering as the lot of the faithful slain for God. Recurrence in Paul lends the echo weight.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand.
echoes.note: Carrying 'the putting to death of Jesus' so that 'life may be revealed' loosely figures the Servant whose death yields life and offspring. The contact is thematic and contested, with no verbal tether, hence figural and low.

pericopes.text: But having the same spirit of faith, according to that which is written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” We also believe, and therefore also we speak; knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus, and will present us with you. For all things are for your sakes, that the grace, being multiplied through the many, may cause the thanksgiving to abound to the glory of God.

echoes.text: I believed, therefore I said, “I was greatly afflicted.”
echoes.note: 'I believed, and therefore I spoke' is an explicit citation (introduced by 'according to that which is written') of the LXX of Psalm 115:1 (MT 116:10). The marked quotation formula and verbatim wording make this an unambiguous quotation.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'He who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also' draws on the OT hope that 'your dead shall live,' the Scriptural seedbed of bodily resurrection. The link is conceptual and shared with Daniel 12:2, so low volume.

pericopes.text: Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory; while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

echoes.text: He said, “Please show me your glory.”
echoes.note: The 'eternal weight of glory' puns on the Hebrew kabod, which means both 'weight' and 'glory,' the very glory Moses asked to see. Paul's running engagement with the Exodus glory theme (chs. 3-4) makes the wordplay plausible, though no verse is quoted.

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.
echoes.note: 'The things which are seen are temporal, but the unseen are eternal' echoes Isaiah's contrast that the heavens and earth 'will vanish away' while God's salvation 'shall be forever.' The transient-visible versus everlasting antithesis aligns well, giving moderate coherence.

echoes.text: who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
echoes.note: The 'inward man renewed day by day' against the decaying outward man faintly echoes the renewal of youth 'like the eagle's.' The contact is thematic and weak, so it serves only as a low-confidence supporting echo.

pericopes.text: For we know that if the earthly house of our tent is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens. For most certainly in this we groan, longing to be clothed with our habitation which is from heaven; if so be that being clothed we will not be found naked. For indeed we who are in this tent do groan, being burdened; not that we desire to be unclothed, but that we desire to be clothed, that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now he who made us for this very thing is God, who also gave to us the down payment of the Spirit.

echoes.text: “Moreover you shall make the tabernacle with ten curtains; of fine twined linen, and blue, and purple, and scarlet, with cherubim. The work of the skillful workman you shall make them. The length of each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits: all the curtains shall have one measure. Five curtains shall be coupled together one to another; and the other five curtains shall be coupled one to another. You shall make […]
echoes.note: The 'earthly house of our tent' (skenos) plays on the tabernacle/tent (skene) of the wilderness, a man-made dwelling contrasted with the 'house not made with hands.' Volume and coherence are moderate: Paul deliberately sets the impermanent, hand-built tent over against an eternal heavenly dwelling, echoing Israel's portable sanctuary. The earthly-vs-eternal sanctuary contrast is thematically apt.
