echoes.text: My dwelling is removed, and is carried away from me like a shepherd’s tent. I have rolled up, like a weaver, my life. He will cut me off from the loom. From day even to night you will make an end of me.
echoes.note: Hezekiah laments 'my dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent,' the body/life imaged as a collapsible tent that is struck down. Paul's 'earthly house of our tent is dissolved' shares the precise tent-as-mortal-life metaphor and the language of dissolution. Volume is modest but the conceptual match (tent = perishable bodily life) is striking.

echoes.text: For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, And the earthy frame lies heavy on a mind that is full of cares.
echoes.note: Wisdom: 'a perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthly tent (geodes skenos) burdens the thoughtful mind.' Paul's 'we who are in this tent do groan, being burdened' (barynomenoi) reproduces both the rare word skenos and the burden motif. High volume and verbal coherence make this the strongest Second-Temple echo in the pericope; availability is secure (Wisdom widely read).

echoes.text: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
echoes.note: The dread of being 'found naked' and the desire to be 'clothed' evokes Adam and Eve's discovery of nakedness and their covering after the fall. Paul does not want to be 'unclothed' but further clothed, reversing the shame of Eden's nakedness with a heavenly garment. Coherence with Paul's new-creation theme (5:17) supports the figural reading.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: The 'down payment of the Spirit' as God's pledge guaranteeing future life draws on the prophetic promise that God will put his Spirit within his people. Ezekiel's gift-of-the-Spirit as eschatological assurance coheres with Paul's arrabon, the Spirit given now as surety of the resurrection body. Recurrence: Paul uses the same Spirit-guarantee logic at 1:22.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.
echoes.note: Joel's promise that God will 'pour out my Spirit on all flesh' stands behind the eschatological gift of the Spirit Paul names as down payment. The link is thematic (the Spirit as the marker of the last days) rather than verbal, so volume is low and the connection is contested against Ezekiel's more personal Spirit-indwelling promise.

pericopes.text: Therefore we are always confident and know that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight. We are courageous, I say, and are willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be at home with the Lord. Therefore also we make it our aim, whether at home or absent, to be well pleasing to him. For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ; that each one may receive the things in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'We walk by faith, not by sight' restates the Habakkuk principle that the righteous live by faith/faithfulness, a text Paul cites programmatically elsewhere (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11). The verbal echo is loose but the theological content—life ordered by trust rather than visible evidence—coheres tightly with Habakkuk's contrast between the proud who rely on sight and the faithful who wait.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: God speaks with Moses 'mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in dark speech,' and Moses 'beholds the form of the LORD'—the privileged sight Paul defers until the believer is 'at home with the Lord.' The faith-now / sight-later structure faintly recalls the Moses-vs-ordinary-prophet distinction. Low volume; contested as a general topos of seeing God rather than a targeted allusion.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's conclusion that 'God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil' is closely paralleled by 'each one may receive the things in the body... whether good or bad.' The good/evil pairing and universal accounting are strongly coherent; high volume of shared content makes the judgment-of-deeds echo secure.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: 'You repay everyone according to what they have done' supplies the recompense logic of the judgment seat where each receives according to deeds. Recurrence is notable: this 'render according to works' formula recurs across the OT (Prov 24:12; Jer 17:10) and Paul invokes it at Rom 2:6, supporting its presence here.

echoes.text: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?
echoes.note: 'Will he not repay everyone according to their deeds?'—God who weighs the heart renders to each by works, matching the judgment-seat recompense. The proverb's emphasis that God sees and requites secret action coheres with Paul's 'revealed before the judgment seat.' Part of a recurrent OT recompense cluster behind 5:10.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds.' The heart-searching judge who recompenses deeds undergirds Paul's appearance before Christ's judgment seat. Coherent with the recompense motif and reinforced by recurrence across the OT requital tradition.

pericopes.text: Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade men, but we are revealed to God; and I hope that we are revealed also in your consciences. For we are not commending ourselves to you again, but speak as giving you occasion of boasting on our behalf, that you may have something to answer those who boast in appearance, and not in heart. For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God. Or if we are of sober mind, it is for you. For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died. He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: 'Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord' echoes the wisdom maxim that 'the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.' Paul grounds his persuasion of others in this reverent fear, coherent with the judgment-seat context just prior. The phrase is a recognizable wisdom formula, supporting a deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom. The knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
echoes.note: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom' is a near-doublet of Prov 1:7 and equally available behind Paul's 'fear of the Lord.' Lower confidence because it adds little beyond the 1:7 echo; flagged for recurrence of the fear-of-the-LORD wisdom topos.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh. His delight will be in the fear of Yahweh. He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears;
echoes.note: The Spirit of 'the fear of the LORD' rests on the messianic shoot, whose 'delight is in the fear of the LORD.' Paul's 'fear of the Lord,' now possibly Christological (fear of/before Christ as judge), faintly recalls this messianic endowment. Volume is low and the link contested against the plainer wisdom-saying source.

pericopes.text: Therefore we know no one after the flesh from now on. Even though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now we know him so no more. Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new. But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation; namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.

echoes.text: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
echoes.note: 'Do not remember the former things... behold, I am doing a new thing' stands directly behind 'the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.' The pairing of forgotten old / heralded new with the demonstrative 'behold' gives high verbal volume and coherence; the new-creation announcement is unmistakably Isaianic second-exodus language.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: 'I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered' supplies both the new-creation (kaine ktisis) vocabulary and the 'former things not remembered' formula echoed in 5:17. High coherence: Paul reads being 'in Christ' as participation in Isaiah's promised new creation; strong availability and thematic fit.

echoes.text: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.
echoes.note: 'The new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me'—the enduring new creation reinforces the new-creation motif of 5:17. Recurrence within Isaiah's new-creation cluster (43; 65; 66) strengthens the case that Paul draws on this stream, though 65:17 is the closer verbal match.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'New creation' (kaine ktisis) figurally recalls the original creation account: being in Christ inaugurates a fresh creative act of God. The link is conceptual and faint, mediated through Isaiah's new-creation language rather than direct verbal contact, so it is marked low and contested.

pericopes.text: We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The herald announcing peace stands behind Paul's role as 'ambassador' through whom God makes his appeal of reconciliation. The envoy/herald-of-peace motif coheres with the ministry of reconciliation, but the verbal contact is faint, so the echo is marked low.

echoes.text: Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions, even all their sins; and he shall put them on the head of the goat, and shall send him away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is in readiness. The goat shall carry all their iniquities on himself to a solitary land, and he shall let the goat go in the wilderness.
echoes.note: 'He made him to be sin' draws on the Day of Atonement, where Israel's sins are laid on the offering and borne away. The cultic 'made to be sin/sin offering' (LXX often renders the sin offering simply as 'sin,' hamartia) underlies Paul's paradox. Coherence with the atoning-exchange logic of 5:21 supports the sacrificial allusion.

echoes.text: He shall lay his hand on the head of the goat, and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before Yahweh. It is a sin offering.
echoes.note: The sin offering (hattat / LXX hamartia) is the technical sacrifice 'for sin'; the LXX's use of the same word for both 'sin' and 'sin offering' lets Paul say God made the sinless Christ 'to be sin.' The double sense undergirds the substitutionary exchange, giving medium volume through the shared Greek term.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all'—the Servant bearing the sin of others is the template for 'he made him to be sin on our behalf.' High coherence with Paul's vicarious exchange and the wider Servant theology of 2 Corinthians; volume of the substitutionary motif is strong.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand.
echoes.note: The Servant's life is made 'an offering for sin' (asham / LXX 'sin'), precisely the sacrificial-exchange logic of 'made him to be sin... so that we might become the righteousness of God.' The sin-offering wording and the resulting vindication of 'the many' give high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: 'The righteous one, my servant, shall make many to be accounted righteous' directly anticipates 'so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.' The righteousness-conferred-on-the-many through the Servant's sin-bearing is a tight thematic and lexical match, the climactic Servant echo behind 5:21.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The Servant 'bore the sin of many' and was 'numbered with the transgressors,' supporting the one-for-all sin-bearing exchange of 5:21 (and 'one died for all,' 5:14). Recurrence across Isaiah 53 (vv. 6, 10, 11, 12) strengthens the overall Servant-song dependence of the pericope.

pericopes.text: Working together, we entreat also that you not receive the grace of God in vain, for he says, “At an acceptable time I listened to you, in a day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, “In an acceptable time have I answered you, and in a day of salvation have I helped you; and I will preserve you, and give you for a covenant of the people, to raise up the land, to make them inherit the desolate heritage:
echoes.note: Verbatim LXX citation introduced by 'he says': 'In an acceptable time I listened to you, in a day of salvation I helped you.' Volume is maximal (explicit formula-marked quotation), recurrence high (Isaiah's Servant Songs pervade Paul's ministry self-understanding), coherence strong as Paul reapplies the eschatological 'day of salvation' to the now of gospel proclamation.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The immediate Servant-Song context that Paul draws on includes the Servant as light/salvation to the nations; faint contextual echo since Paul's apostolic role mirrors the Servant's commissioning. Volume low (not quoted), but availability and coherence with v.2's quotation support a contextual reading.

pericopes.text: We give no occasion of stumbling in anything, that our service may not be blamed, but in everything commending ourselves, as servants of God, in great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses, in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in watchings, in fastings; in pureness, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; by the armor of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, by glory and dishonor, by evil report and good report; as deceivers, and yet true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.

echoes.text: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.
echoes.note: The hardship catalog of the suffering-yet-delivered righteous one ('many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all') stands behind Paul's peristasis. Coherence is strong with the righteous-sufferer topos; recurrence high in Paul, though volume is diffuse rather than a marked citation.

echoes.text: I will not die, but live, and declare Yah’s works. Yah has punished me severely, but he has not given me over to death.
echoes.note: 'As dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and not killed' closely tracks 'I shall not die, but live... The LORD has chastened me severely, but he has not given me over to death.' Volume moderate (no formula, but distinctive paired antithesis of chastening-yet-not-killed), coherence high with paschal deliverance language Paul applies to apostolic survival.

echoes.text: I run in the path of your commandments, for you have set my heart free.
echoes.note: The motif of endurance and the enlarged heart (anticipating v.11) under affliction has loose verbal contact with the psalmist running the way of commandments 'when you enlarge my heart.' Faint; volume low and the connection is thematic, included for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting. For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed. He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me.
echoes.note: The Servant's vindication amid beatings and dishonor ('I gave my back to those who strike... he who vindicates me is near') coheres with Paul's 'by glory and dishonor, by evil report and good report.' Volume low and diffuse, but availability strong given the chapter's Isaiah-49 anchor.

echoes.text: There are some who pretend to be rich, yet have nothing. There are some who pretend to be poor, yet have great wealth.
echoes.note: 'As poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things' echoes the proverbial paradox 'One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.' Volume low, contested as a possible sapiential commonplace rather than a deliberate citation.

pericopes.text: Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians. Our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted by your own affections. Now in return, I speak as to my children, you also be open wide.

echoes.text: I run in the path of your commandments, for you have set my heart free.
echoes.note: 'Our heart is enlarged' / 'be open wide' uses the idiom of the enlarged (widened) heart found in 'I will run the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart.' Volume low and the metaphor is common, but the shared verb of heart-widening gives a faint, plausible contact.

echoes.text: Be careful, lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside, and serve other gods, and worship them;
echoes.note: Paul's plea against the heart being 'restricted' / led astray by their own affections faintly recalls Deuteronomy's warnings to guard the heart from being deceived. Very faint; included only for maximal coverage and bridges to the holiness summons of vv.14-18.

pericopes.text: Don’t be unequally yoked with unbelievers, for what fellowship have righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?

echoes.text: You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.
echoes.note: 'Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers' draws on the law against plowing with an ox and a donkey yoked together as the figural ground of the metaphor heterozygountes. Volume strong (the rare yoking image), coherence high with separation theology, availability secure in Torah.

echoes.text: “‘You shall keep my statutes. “‘You shall not cross-breed different kinds of animals. “‘You shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed; “‘neither shall there come upon you a garment made of two kinds of material.
echoes.note: The holiness-code ban on mixing kinds (breeding cattle of two kinds, mixed seed, mixed garments) underlies the 'unequally yoked' prohibition Paul applies to believers and unbelievers. Coherence high with the Levitical separation logic that governs the whole catena; the LXX heterozyga term in Lev 19:19 verbally anchors the allusion.

echoes.text: Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, and wickedness as with cart rope; Who say, “Let him make speed, let him hasten his work, that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, that we may know it!” Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil; who put darkness for light, and light for darkness; who put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
echoes.note: The antithesis of righteousness vs. lawlessness and light vs. darkness loosely recalls Isaiah's woes on those who 'call darkness light and light darkness.' Volume low; the light/darkness dualism is widespread (cf. Qumran), so this is a contested availability echo.

pericopes.text: What agreement has a temple of God with idols? For you are a temple of the living God. Even as God said, “I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they will be my people.”

echoes.text: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: 'I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they will be my people' fuses Lev 26:12 ('I will walk among you and be your God, and you shall be my people') as the lead text of the catena. Volume maximal (formula-marked 'as God said'), coherence high with the temple-of-the-living-God claim, availability secure.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: The conflated citation also draws Ezekiel's new-covenant promise 'My dwelling place shall be with them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people'; the 'dwelling/tabernacle among them' language is closer to Ezekiel than Leviticus. A genuine second link of the catena, high volume and coherence within the temple theme.

echoes.text: neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions; but I will save them out of all their dwelling places, in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God.
echoes.note: The adjacent verse promising cleansing from idols ('they shall not defile themselves anymore with their idols') resonates with Paul's 'what agreement has a temple of God with idols?' Volume low, but coherent contextual support for the Ezekiel 37 source.

pericopes.text: Therefore “‘Come out from among them, and be separate,’ says the Lord. ‘Touch no unclean thing. I will receive you.

echoes.text: Depart, depart, go out from there, touch no unclean thing! Go out of the midst of her! Cleanse yourselves, you who bear the vessels of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Come out from among them, and be separate, says the Lord, touch no unclean thing' quotes 'Depart, depart, go out from there, touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her, purify yourselves.' Volume maximal (formula-marked), coherence high with the exodus/return-from-exile separation summons; availability secure.

echoes.text: and I will bring you out from the peoples, and will gather you out of the countries in which you are scattered, with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out;
echoes.note: 'I will receive you' (eisdexomai) matches Ezekiel's promise to gather and receive the people out from the peoples ('I will bring you out... and I will receive you'), supplying the welcome-clause not present in Isaiah 52:11. Volume moderate via the distinctive verb; a real catena link.

echoes.text: As a pleasant aroma will I accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples, and gather you out of the countries in which you have been scattered; and I will be sanctified in you in the sight of the nations.
echoes.note: The parallel 'I will receive you' in Ezek 20:41 ('I will accept you as a pleasing aroma when I bring you out') reinforces the source of Paul's reception-promise tied to separation from defilement. Coherence high with the holiness/return motif.

echoes.text: At that time will I bring you in, and at that time will I gather you; for I will give you honor and praise among all the peoples of the earth, when I restore your fortunes before your eyes, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'At that time I will bring you in... I will gather you' offers another gathering/reception promise that may stand behind the welcome clause. Volume low and overlaps with the Ezekiel material; contested but plausible for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans. With a voice of singing declare, tell this, utter it even to the end of the earth: say, Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob.
echoes.note: 'Go out from Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans' is a parallel exodus-summons in Deutero-Isaiah reinforcing the 'come out and be separate' imperative. Faint and overlapping with 52:11; included as a low-confidence availability echo.

pericopes.text: I will be to you a Father. You will be to me sons and daughters,’ says the Lord Almighty.”

echoes.text: I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men;
echoes.note: 'I will be to you a Father. You will be to me sons and daughters' adapts the Davidic-covenant promise 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son,' pluralized and expanded to the community. Volume high (formula-marked 'says the Lord Almighty'), coherence high as the covenant-sonship climax of the catena.

echoes.text: I will tell the north, ‘Give them up!’ and tell the south, ‘Don’t hold them back! Bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth—
echoes.note: The plural 'sons and daughters' ('Bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth') supplies the gendered expansion absent from 2 Sam 7:14. Volume moderate via the distinctive 'sons and daughters' pairing; a genuine conflated link coherent with the gathering theme of v.17.

echoes.text: They shall come with weeping; and with petitions will I lead them: I will cause them to walk by rivers of waters, in a straight way in which they shall not stumble; for I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.
echoes.note: 'I am a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn' provides the fatherhood-to-the-people motif within the new-covenant chapter Paul elsewhere prizes. Volume moderate, coherence high with the new-covenant framing of 2 Corinthians 3 and this catena.

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'In the place where it was said... 'You are not my people,' it shall be said... 'Sons of the living God'' links the sonship promise to the 'living God' temple language of v.16 and the not-my-people/my-people reversal. Volume moderate, coherence strong; Paul cites this elsewhere (Rom 9:26), raising availability and recurrence.

pericopes.text: Having therefore these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

echoes.text: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth. For I am Yahweh who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
echoes.note: Paul's call to 'perfect holiness' (cleansing from defilement) draws on the Holiness Code's central formula 'be holy, for I am holy,' which grounds Israel's purity in God's holiness. Coherence is strong with Paul's preceding temple-of-God argument (6:16-18), and the cleansing-for-holiness logic matches Leviticus directly. Volume is moderate since Paul does not quote, but the conceptual fusion of cleansing and consecration is distinctly Levitical.

echoes.text: Wash yourselves, make yourself clean. Put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes. Cease to do evil.
echoes.note: Isaiah's prophetic summons 'wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your deeds' supplies the ethical-cleansing register Paul uses against 'defilement of flesh and spirit.' The echo moves the cultic language of purity into moral self-purification, exactly Isaiah's prophetic move. Recurrence of Isaiah elsewhere in the chapter (49:13 below) strengthens the case for availability and authorial intent.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's promise 'I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses' is the closest OT antecedent for cleansing from 'all defilement,' especially since 36:26-27 supplies the new-covenant Spirit Paul invokes throughout 2 Cor 3-7. The pairing of cleansing with the Spirit ('defilement of flesh and spirit') coheres tightly with Ezekiel's water-and-Spirit sequence. Volume is moderate; the link rests on shared cleansing-plus-Spirit logic rather than verbal quotation.

echoes.text: Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: The temple-ascent question 'who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart' parallels Paul's pairing of bodily and spiritual cleansing as prerequisite for holiness before God. Given the preceding temple imagery (6:16), the figural fit is real but the volume is faint and the language general. Marked low and contested because purity-of-heart language is widespread.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: Paul completes holiness 'in the fear of God,' the wisdom tradition's foundational posture ('the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge'). The phrase is idiomatic across the OT, so volume is low and recurrence diffuse, but the wisdom resonance is genuine and coheres with Paul's ethical exhortation. Contested because 'fear of God' is a stock biblical idiom rather than a specific citation.

pericopes.text: Open your hearts to us. We wronged no one. We corrupted no one. We took advantage of no one. I say this not to condemn you, for I have said before, that you are in our hearts to die together and live together. Great is my boldness of speech toward you. Great is my boasting on your behalf. I am filled with comfort. I overflow with joy in all our affliction.

echoes.text: Here I am. Witness against me before Yahweh, and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Of whose hand have I taken a ransom to blind my eyes therewith? I will restore it to you.” They said, “You have not defrauded us, nor oppressed us, neither have you taken anything of any man’s hand.”
echoes.note: Paul's threefold self-vindication 'we wronged no one, we corrupted no one, we took advantage of no one' echoes Samuel's farewell defense before Israel ('whom have I wronged? whom have I oppressed? from whose hand have I taken a bribe?'). Both are leaders asserting integrity against a congregation amid suspicion, a strong coherence of setting. Volume is moderate: the rhetorical form of a serial disavowal of exploitation is the shared feature rather than exact wording.

pericopes.text: For even when we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no relief, but we were afflicted on every side. Fightings were outside. Fear was inside. Nevertheless, he who comforts the lowly, God, comforted us by the coming of Titus; and not by his coming only, but also by the comfort with which he was comforted in you, while he told us of your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me; so that I rejoiced still more.

echoes.text: Sing, heavens; and be joyful, earth; and break out into singing, mountains: for Yahweh has comforted his people, and will have compassion on his afflicted.
echoes.note: Paul's title for God, 'he who comforts the lowly/downcast,' closely renders Isaiah 49:13 ('the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted'), part of the Servant-Songs comfort tradition Paul mines throughout 2 Corinthians. The verbal link of God-comforting-the-afflicted is high in volume, and Isaiah's recurrence across the letter (and within this chapter) satisfies availability and recurrence. Coherence is strong: Paul casts his own affliction-and-comfort in Isaian terms.

echoes.text: “Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God.
echoes.note: The programmatic 'comfort, comfort my people, says your God' underlies the whole consolation vocabulary of 2 Cor 1-7 and resurfaces here in 'God comforted us.' Recurrence is strong because Paul's repeated paraklesis language draws on Deutero-Isaiah's comfort oracle. Volume here is moderate, since 49:13 is the nearer verbal parallel and 40:1 supplies the broader thematic frame.

echoes.text: As one whom his mother comforts, so will I comfort you; and you will be comforted in Jerusalem.”
echoes.note: 'As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you' is part of the same Isaian comfort cluster as 49:13 and may stand behind Paul's God-who-comforts language. Volume is faint and it overlaps heavily with the stronger 49:13 link, so it is marked low and contested. Listed for completeness of the Isaian consolation field.

echoes.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the ash heap; that he may set him with princes, even with the princes of his people.
echoes.note: God 'who comforts the lowly' resonates with the psalmic motif of God raising the poor from the dust and lifting the needy to sit with princes. The reversal-of-the-lowly theme coheres with Paul's self-description as cast down then comforted, but the volume is low and the link is conceptual rather than verbal. Contested as a general lowliness-exaltation topos.

echoes.text: so that he sets up on high those who are low, those who mourn are exalted to safety.
echoes.note: 'He sets on high those who are lowly, and those who mourn are lifted to safety' parallels Paul's 'God who comforts the lowly' alongside the Corinthians' 'mourning' (7:7). The shared lowly-and-mourning pairing is suggestive, but Job is rarely echoed by Paul and the volume is faint. Marked low and contested.

pericopes.text: For though I made you sorry with my letter, I do not regret it, though I did regret it. For I see that my letter made you sorry, though just for a while. I now rejoice, not that you were made sorry, but that you were made sorry to repentance. For you were made sorry in a godly way, that you might suffer loss by us in nothing. For godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world works death. For behold, this same thing, that you were made sorry in a godly way, what earnest care it worked in you. Yes, what defense, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and vengeance! In everything you demonstrated yourselves to be pure in the matter. So although I wrote to you, I wrote not for his cause that did the wrong, nor for his cause that suffered the wrong, but that your earnest care for us might be revealed in you in the sight of God. Therefore we have been comforted. In our comfort we rejoiced the more exceedingly for the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all.

echoes.text: “Yet even now,” says Yahweh, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.
echoes.note: Paul's contrast of 'godly grief that produces repentance' against 'worldly grief that produces death' draws on the prophetic repentance tradition where genuine turning is inward ('return to me with all your heart... rend your hearts and not your garments'). Joel's heart-repentance leading to life coheres with Paul's salvation-bringing sorrow. Volume is moderate and conceptual, resting on the prophetic repentance schema rather than wording.

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me. Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge. Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin […]
echoes.note: The paradigm of godly sorrow yielding repentance unto salvation evokes David's penitential psalm, where 'a broken and contrite heart' is the sacrifice God accepts and the path to restored salvation (51:12, 17). Coherence with Paul's salvific, non-regretted sorrow is strong; volume is moderate since Paul alludes to the penitential pattern rather than quoting. The contrite-heart-unto-restoration logic is the shared structure.

echoes.text: There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.
echoes.note: 'There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death' parallels Paul's 'the sorrow of the world produces death,' the wisdom antithesis of two ways ending in life or death. The death-as-terminus motif coheres, but the volume is faint and the link conceptual. Marked low and contested as a general two-ways topos.

pericopes.text: For if in anything I have boasted to him on your behalf, I was not disappointed. But as we spoke all things to you in truth, so our glorying also which I made before Titus was found to be truth. His affection is more abundantly toward you, while he remembers all of your obedience, how with fear and trembling you received him. I rejoice that in everything I am confident concerning you.

echoes.text: Serve Yahweh with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
echoes.note: The Corinthians received Titus 'with fear and trembling,' a phrase whose OT home includes 'serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling.' Paul uses fear-and-trembling elsewhere as a posture of reverent obedience, so the idiom likely carries a Septuagintal coloring here. Volume is low and the phrase is a stock biblical collocation, so it is marked low and contested.

pericopes.text: Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia; how that in much proof of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their liberality. For according to their power, I testify, yes and beyond their power, they gave of their own accord, begging us with much entreaty to receive this grace and the fellowship in the service to the saints. This was not as we had hoped, but first they gave their own selves to the Lord, and to us through the will of God. So we urged Titus, that as he made a beginning before, so he would also complete in you this grace. But as you abound in everything, in faith, utterance, knowledge, all earnestness, and in your love to us, see that you also abound in this grace.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: Paul's appeal that the Macedonians gave generously out of deep poverty rests on the Deuteronomic open-hand command: do not harden your heart against the poor brother but give freely. The 'fellowship in service to the saints' (v.4) reflects the same covenantal obligation to relieve a needy member of God's people. Coherence with the whole collection theme is high, though the verbal link is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
echoes.note: The paradox that the Macedonians' deep poverty 'abounded to the riches of their liberality' (v.2) echoes the wisdom maxim that one who scatters yet increases and the liberal soul is made rich. The generosity-brings-abundance reversal is a recurring sapiential theme Paul draws on through the chapter; volume is modest, coherence strong.

echoes.text: ‘Take from among you an offering to Yahweh. Whoever is of a willing heart, let him bring it, Yahweh’s offering: gold, silver, brass,
echoes.note: The Macedonians giving 'of their own accord' and begging to share in the collection (vv.3-4) recalls the willing-hearted offering for the tabernacle, where everyone whose heart stirred him brought a freewill gift. The collection-for-the-sanctuary typology underlies Paul's framing of the Jerusalem fund as a sacred offering. Faint and contested as a deliberate echo.

pericopes.text: I speak not by way of commandment, but as proving through the earnestness of others the sincerity also of your love. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. I give a judgment in this: for this is expedient for you, who were the first to start a year ago, not only to do, but also to be willing. But now complete the doing also, that as there was the readiness to be willing, so there may be the completion also out of your ability. For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what you have, not according to what you don’t have.

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: The summons to a willing readiness in giving 'according to what you have' (vv.11-12) resonates with the blessing on the bountiful eye that gives bread to the poor. The wisdom tradition that values the disposition of the giver over the amount stands behind Paul's stress on willingness; the link is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and […]
echoes.note: The Christological reversal in v.9, 'though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor,' may evoke the Servant who, despised and stripped of form, is poured out and yet by his abasement enriches the many. The pattern of voluntary self-impoverishment for others' gain coheres with Isaiah's Servant, but the conceptual frame of pre-existent riches is Pauline rather than verbal Isaianic; contested.

pericopes.text: For this is not that others may be eased and you distressed, but for equality. Your abundance at this present time supplies their lack, that their abundance also may become a supply for your lack; that there may be equality. As it is written, “He who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack.”

echoes.text: When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They gathered every man according to his eating.
echoes.note: Verse 15 explicitly quotes ('as it is written') the manna narrative: 'He who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack.' Paul lifts the LXX wording of the equalizing of the manna to ground his principle of economic equality among the assemblies. Volume, explicit citation formula, and coherence with the equality theme are all maximal.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has become poor, and his hand can’t support himself among you; then you shall uphold him. He shall live with you like an alien and a temporary resident. Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God; that your brother may live among you. You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit.
echoes.note: The principle of 'equality' so that one's abundance supplies another's lack (vv.13-14) resonates with the Jubilee/sabbatical ethic of sustaining the impoverished brother without profit. The leveling vision behind Paul's mutual-supply argument is at home in the Holiness Code's economy of need; faint and thematic.

pericopes.text: But thanks be to God, who puts the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus. For he indeed accepted our exhortation, but being himself very earnest, he went out to you of his own accord. We have sent together with him the brother whose praise in the Good News is known through all the assemblies. Not only so, but who was also appointed by the assemblies to travel with us in this grace, which is served by us to the glory of the Lord himself, and to show our readiness. We are avoiding this, that any man should blame us concerning this abundance which is administered by us. Having regard for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. We have sent with them our brother, whom we have many times proved earnest in many things, but now much more earnest, by reason of the great confidence which he has in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for you. As for our brothers, they are the apostles of the assemblies, the glory of Christ. Therefore show the proof of your love to them in front of the assemblies, and of our boasting on your behalf.

echoes.text: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
echoes.note: Verse 21, 'Having regard for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men,' closely follows LXX Proverbs 3:4, 'provide for good things in the sight of the Lord and of men.' Paul applies the maxim of seeking favor and good repute before God and humans to his transparent handling of the collection. The lexical overlap (good/honorable things; sight of Lord and men) gives high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: A servant who deals wisely will rule over a son who causes shame, and shall have a part in the inheritance among the brothers.
echoes.note: The care to be above blame in administering the gift (v.20), guarding the apostles' reputation, draws on the wisdom concern for the faithful steward who avoids reproach. The administrative-integrity motif is sapiential but the link to any single proverb is diffuse; faint.

pericopes.text: It is indeed unnecessary for me to write to you concerning the service to the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast on your behalf to them of Macedonia, that Achaia has been prepared for a year past. Your zeal has stirred up very many of them. But I have sent the brothers that our boasting on your behalf may not be in vain in this respect, that, just as I said, you may be prepared, so that I won’t by any means, if there come with me any of Macedonia and find you unprepared, we (to say nothing of you) should be disappointed in this confident boasting. I thought it necessary therefore to entreat the brothers that they would go before to you, and arrange ahead of time the generous gift that you promised before, that the same might be ready as a matter of generosity, and not of greediness.

echoes.text: Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it.
echoes.note: Paul calls the collection a 'generous gift' using eulogia (blessing/bounty), the same Septuagintal idiom by which Jacob presses his 'blessing' (gift) on Esau. The lexical overlap is suggestive rather than demonstrable, since eulogia-as-present is a stock LXX usage available to Paul. Coherence is moderate: Paul frames almsgiving as a transferable blessing, exactly the Genesis nuance.

echoes.text: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty.
echoes.note: Paul's contrast between a gift given 'as a matter of generosity, and not of greediness (pleonexia)' anticipates the wisdom antithesis between the open hand that grows richer and the withholding that brings want. Volume is faint here because the proverbial sowing language proper surfaces in 9:6, but the generosity/covetousness polarity is already in view. Marked contested as a generic sapiential register.

pericopes.text: Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart; not grudgingly, or under compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver.

echoes.text: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself. People curse someone who withholds grain, but blessing will be on the head of him who sells it.
echoes.note: Paul's maxim that sparing sowing yields sparing reaping while bountiful sowing yields bountiful reaping closely tracks the wisdom paradox 'one gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want.' Coherence is strong since both texts treat almsgiving under an agricultural-recompense logic, and the bountiful-eye blessing of 22:9 reinforces availability. Volume is high at the conceptual level even though Paul does not quote verbatim.

echoes.text: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed. He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: The sowing-and-reaping figure plus the 'bountiful eye' that is blessed for giving bread to the poor (22:8-9) supplies both halves of Paul's argument here and into v.7. The LXX expansion of 22:8 ('God blesses a cheerful man and a giver') is the most probable direct source of 'God loves a cheerful giver,' giving high recurrence and coherence across vv.6-7. Availability is secure since Paul cites Proverbs elsewhere.
echoes.lxxText: He that sows wickedness shall reap troubles; and shall fully receive the punishment of his deeds. God loves a cheerful and liberal man; but a man shall fully prove the folly of his works. He that has pity on the poor shall himself be maintained; for he has given of his own bread to the poor. He that gives liberally secures victory an honour; but he takes away the life of them that posses them.

echoes.text: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed.
echoes.note: The clause 'God loves a cheerful giver' has no Hebrew counterpart but matches the Septuagintal plus to Proverbs 22:8b, 'God blesses a cheerful man and a giver,' nearly word for word in vocabulary (hilaron, didonta/doten). The verbal volume is high enough that most commentators treat this as Paul's source rather than free composition. The shift from 'blesses' to 'loves' is the only material variation.
echoes.lxxText: He that sows wickedness shall reap troubles; and shall fully receive the punishment of his deeds. God loves a cheerful and liberal man; but a man shall fully prove the folly of his works.

echoes.text: You shall surely give, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him; because that for this thing Yahweh your God will bless you in all your work, and in all that you put your hand to.
echoes.note: Paul's prohibition of giving 'grudgingly or under compulsion' echoes the Deuteronomic command to give to the poor 'and your heart shall not be grudging when you give,' with the promise that the LORD will bless you for it. Coherence is strong because both texts attach divine favor to ungrudging almsgiving. Volume is moderate; the shared idea of the un-grudging heart is distinctive enough to exceed a commonplace.

echoes.text: Glorify the Lord with a good eye, And stint not the first fruits of your hands. In every gift show a cheerful countenance, And dedicate your tithe with gladness. Give to the Most High according as he has given; And as your hand has found, give with a good eye. For the Lord recompenses, And he will recompense you sevenfold.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's instruction to glorify the Lord with a generous gift, give 'with a cheerful eye/face,' and not to be sparing because the Lord repays is a strikingly close Second-Temple parallel to Paul's cheerful, ungrudging giver. Availability and coherence are high; recurrence is supported by Sirach's wider almsgiving theology. Marked medium since Paul's nearer verbal source remains Proverbs 22:8 LXX.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: The prophetic summons to 'sow for yourselves righteousness, reap steadfast love' supplies the moralized sowing/reaping pattern Paul deploys, where the harvest is a moral-spiritual yield, not mere produce. Coherence is strong with v.10's 'fruits of your righteousness,' and recurrence within the chapter strengthens the case. Volume is moderate because Hosea's specific righteousness/mercy pairing surfaces more explicitly at v.10.

echoes.text: According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity, and sow trouble, reap the same.
echoes.note: Eliphaz's observation that 'those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same' is the negative form of Paul's reciprocity principle. The connection is thematic rather than verbal, and the moral valence is inverted (Job warns of bad harvests), so volume and coherence are limited. Included as a maximal flag for the broader OT sowing-reaping topos.

echoes.text: My son, sow not upon the furrows of unrighteousness, And you shall not reap them sevenfold.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's 'do not sow in the furrows of injustice, lest you reap them sevenfold' offers a Second-Temple instance of the sowing-reaping recompense Paul assumes. Availability is good but the volume is faint and the link conceptual, since Sirach frames the negative (injustice) while Paul frames generosity positively. Marked contested as background topos rather than source.

pericopes.text: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work. As it is written, “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.” Now may he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed for sowing, and increase the fruits of your righteousness; you being enriched in everything to all liberality, which works through us thanksgiving to God.

echoes.text: He has dispersed, he has given to the poor. His righteousness endures forever. His horn will be exalted with honor.
echoes.note: Paul introduces with the formula 'as it is written' and cites Psalm 112:9 (LXX 111:9) verbatim: 'He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.' The verbal volume is maximal and the citation explicit, the clearest OT quotation in the chapter. Coherence is strong: the psalm's generous, God-fearing man models the Corinthians' almsgiving, and 'his righteousness' bridges to v.10's harvest of righteousness.

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater;
echoes.note: Paul's description of God as the one 'who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food' draws directly on Isaiah's image of rain that gives 'seed to the sower and bread to the eater,' the only OT verse pairing both phrases. Volume is high through the doubled, distinctive word-pair, and coherence is strong since Isaiah's seed/word fruitfulness underlies Paul's promise that God will multiply the seed. Availability is secure given Paul's heavy use of Isaiah 40-66.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: The promise to 'increase the fruits of your righteousness' reprises Hosea's 'sow righteousness, reap steadfast love,' where righteousness is precisely the crop. Coherence is strong because Paul fuses the agricultural supply of v.10 with a moral harvest, exactly Hosea's move. Volume is moderate; the phrase 'fruit/harvest of righteousness' is a shared idiom rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. He who is wise wins souls.
echoes.note: Paul's 'fruits of your righteousness' resonates with the wisdom maxim 'the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life,' part of the same sapiential harvest imagery. The link is idiomatic and faint relative to Hosea 10:12, so volume is low and the source contested. Flagged for completeness within the righteousness-as-fruit cluster.

echoes.text: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.
echoes.note: God's supplying 'bread for food' (v.10) coheres with the creation psalm's praise of the LORD who brings forth 'food from the earth' and 'bread to strengthen the heart of man.' The thematic overlap of divine provision of bread is real but generic, so volume is faint and the connection contested. Isaiah 55:10 remains the stronger candidate.

echoes.text: You shall surely give, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him; because that for this thing Yahweh your God will bless you in all your work, and in all that you put your hand to.
echoes.note: Paul's assurance that the cheerful giver is 'enriched in everything to all liberality' echoes the Deuteronomic promise that the LORD 'will bless you in all your work' because you give to the poor. Coherence with the chapter's almsgiving theology is good, but the verbal contact is slight, so volume is low. Marked contested as a continuation of the v.7 Deuteronomy stratum.

echoes.text: The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
echoes.note: The sapiential principle that 'the liberal soul shall be made fat, and he who waters will himself be watered' parallels Paul's promise that giving leads to being 'enriched in everything.' The reciprocal-blessing logic matches, but the link is conceptual and contested rather than verbal. Included as a maximal flag in the generosity-enrichment cluster.

pericopes.text: For this service of giving that you perform not only makes up for lack among the saints, but abounds also through many givings of thanks to God; seeing that through the proof given by this service, they glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Good News of Christ, and for the liberality of your contribution to them and to all; while they themselves also, with supplication on your behalf, yearn for you by reason of the exceeding grace of God in you. Now thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift!

echoes.text: to appoint to those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of Yahweh, that he may be glorified.
echoes.note: Paul's repeated 'thanksgivings to God' and the people's glorifying God for the gift resonate with Isaiah's vision of the redeemed bringing praise and being called 'oaks of righteousness... that he may be glorified.' The link is thematic (almsgiving issuing in doxology) rather than verbal, so volume is faint. Flagged because Isaiah supplies the broader glory-and-righteousness horizon of the chapter.

echoes.text: Give to the Most High according as he has given; And as your hand has found, give with a good eye. For the Lord recompenses, And he will recompense you sevenfold.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's counsel that giving to the Lord is repaid sevenfold and met with a glad face stands behind Paul's claim that the saints' service overflows in 'many givings of thanks to God.' The almsgiving-thanksgiving circuit is a shared Second-Temple pattern, but the contact is conceptual, hence low volume and contested. Reinforces the Sirach stratum already noted at v.7.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's almsgiving instruction, that giving lays up a good treasure and delivers, supplies a Second-Temple almsgiving theology congruent with Paul's account of the collection as a God-glorifying ministry. The connection is to the wider piety rather than any phrase, so volume is faint and the source contested. Included to map the deuterocanonical background of the collection ethic.

echoes.text: Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it.
echoes.note: Paul's climactic 'thanks be to God for his indescribable gift' may extend the eulogia/gift register of the chapter, but no specific OT text underlies the doxology; the divine gift transcends OT precedent by design. The link to Genesis 33:11 is offered only as the chapter-spanning gift idiom. Very low volume; clearly contested.

pericopes.text: Now I Paul, myself, entreat you by the humility and gentleness of Christ; I who in your presence am lowly among you, but being absent am bold toward you. Yes, I beg you that I may not, when present, show courage with the confidence with which I intend to be bold against some, who consider us to be walking according to the flesh. For though we walk in the flesh, we don’t wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ; and being in readiness to avenge all disobedience, when your obedience will be made full.

echoes.text: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
echoes.note: Paul appeals 'by the humility and gentleness of Christ.' Zechariah's messianic king comes 'humble (meek) and riding on a donkey,' the OT locus most read by early Christians as Christ's defining meekness. The conceptual match (the gentle, lowly Messiah whose authority is non-coercive) gives coherence, but Paul cites no words, so the echo is faint.
echoes.altSource: Numbers 12:3 (Moses 'very meek'); Isaiah 42:2-3 (servant who will not break a bruised reed)

echoes.text: He will not shout, nor raise his voice, nor cause it to be heard in the street. He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick. He will faithfully bring justice.
echoes.note: The Servant 'will not cry out or lift up his voice... a bruised reed he will not break' models the gentleness Paul invokes for Christ. Coherence with Pauline servant-Christology is high, but volume is low and the language is not reproduced, so this is a faint figural backdrop to Christ's 'gentleness.'

echoes.text: A wise man scales the city of the mighty, and brings down the strength of its confidence.
echoes.note: 'A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust' supplies the precise military metaphor Paul redeploys: weapons 'mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds.' The shared verb-idea (a wise/divine power demolishing the fortress of the proud) gives strong volume and coherence with Paul's contrast of fleshly vs. God-empowered warfare.

echoes.text: The lofty looks of man will be brought low, the haughtiness of men will be bowed down, and Yahweh alone will be exalted in that day. For there will be a day of Yahweh of Armies for all that is proud and haughty, and for all that is lifted up; and it shall be brought low: For all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, for all the oaks of Bashan, For all the high mountains, for all the hills that are lifted up, For every lofty tower, for every […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's oracle that 'the haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the LORD alone exalted,' targeting 'every one that is proud and lofty' and 'every high tower,' directly underwrites Paul's 'every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God.' The shared lexicon of loftiness/exaltation humbled before God gives high volume and thematic coherence.

echoes.text: He has brought the high fortress of your walls down, laid low, and brought to the ground, even to the dust.
echoes.note: 'The high fortress of your walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground' couples the very images Paul fuses: high things and strongholds thrown down by God. Recurrence within Isaiah's strongholds-of-pride theme strengthens the case, though Paul names no source.

echoes.text: For he has brought down those who dwell on high, the lofty city. He lays it low. He lays it low even to the ground. He brings it even to the dust.
echoes.note: 'He has brought down those who dwell on high, the lofty city he lays low, even to the ground' restates the casting-down-the-proud motif undergirding 10:5. The recurrence of Isaiah's lofty-city/stronghold language alongside Isaiah 2 and 25 raises the cumulative likelihood that Paul draws on this prophetic stock imagery.

echoes.text: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
echoes.note: Jeremiah's commission 'to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant' frames prophetic authority as power to demolish and to build — the same dual structure Paul invokes (here the destroying side; the building side surfaces in 10:8). Coherence with Paul's apostolic self-understanding is strong, though the destroying half is generic.

echoes.text: Pour out the fury of your anger. Look at everyone who is proud, and bring him low. Look at everyone who is proud, and humble him. Crush the wicked in their place.
echoes.note: God's challenge to 'look on everyone who is proud and abase him... tread down the wicked where they stand' matches Paul's casting down of 'every high thing.' The motif of proud heights leveled is shared, but the link is thematic rather than verbal, so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: For you will save the afflicted people, but the haughty eyes you will bring down.
echoes.note: 'You save a humble people, but haughty eyes you bring down' encapsulates the same reversal — God humbling the lofty — that Paul applies to thoughts 'exalted against the knowledge of God.' Coherence is good but volume low; one of several proud-brought-low texts in the OT stock Paul echoes.

echoes.text: He will take his jealousy as complete armor, And will make the whole creation his weapons for vengeance on his enemies: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet; He will take holiness as an invincible shield, And he will sharpen stern wrath for a sword: And the world will go forth with him to fight against his insensate foes.
echoes.note: God 'will take his zeal as a panoply' and arm creation as weapons against his foes; this Second-Temple militarization of divine 'weapons' parallels Paul's 'weapons of our warfare... mighty before God.' Availability and coherence support an echo of the divine-armor topos, though Paul's vocabulary differs.
echoes.altSource: Isaiah 59:17 (the LORD puts on righteousness as a breastplate)

echoes.text: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you, that you may be no priest to me. Because you have forgotten your God’s law, I will also forget your children.
echoes.note: Paul's phrase 'the knowledge of God' as the contested prize echoes the prophetic idiom where Israel is destroyed 'for lack of knowledge' of God (cf. Hosea 6:6). The theme coheres with Paul's polemic, but the genitive phrase is common biblical idiom, so the echo is faint and contested.

pericopes.text: Do you look at things only as they appear in front of your face? If anyone trusts in himself that he is Christ’s, let him consider this again with himself, that, even as he is Christ’s, so also we are Christ’s. For though I should boast somewhat abundantly concerning our authority, (which the Lord gave for building you up, and not for casting you down) I will not be disappointed, that I may not seem as if I desire to terrify you by my letters. For, “His letters”, they say, “are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised.” Let such a person consider this, that what we are in word by letters when we are absent, such are we also in deed when we are present.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: 'Do you look at things only as they appear in front of your face?' rebukes judgment by outward appearance, the exact contrast of 1 Samuel 16:7: 'man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.' The shared appearance/heart antithesis, applied to who truly belongs to Christ, gives strong coherence and volume.

echoes.text: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
echoes.note: Paul defines his Lord-given authority as 'for building you up, and not for casting you down,' directly drawing on Jeremiah's commission 'to build and to plant' over against 'to break down... and to overthrow.' The build-up/tear-down polarity is distinctively Jeremianic and recurs across Jeremiah, giving high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: For I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them again to this land: and I will build them, and not pull them down; and I will plant them, and not pluck them up.
echoes.note: 'I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not pluck them up' is the positive restoration form of Jeremiah's formula that Paul echoes in 'building up, and not casting down.' Recurrence of this exact build/not-tear-down pairing (also 31:28; 42:10) strengthens the allusion's likelihood.

echoes.text: It shall happen that, like as I have watched over them to pluck up and to break down and to overthrow and to destroy and to afflict, so will I watch over them to build and to plant, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'As I watched over them to pluck up and break down... so I will watch over them to build and to plant' is a further occurrence of the Jeremianic build/destroy idiom behind 10:8. Listed for recurrence; lower confidence since 1:10 and 24:6 already carry the allusion.

pericopes.text: For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding. But we will not boast beyond proper limits, but within the boundaries with which God appointed to us, which reach even to you. For we don’t stretch ourselves too much, as though we didn’t reach to you. For we came even as far as to you with the Good News of Christ, not boasting beyond proper limits in other men’s labors, but having hope that as your faith grows, we will be abundantly enlarged by you in our sphere of influence, so as to preach the Good News even to the parts beyond you, not to boast in what someone else has already done. But “he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.” For it isn’t he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends.

echoes.text: Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
echoes.note: 'Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips' is the proverbial backbone of Paul's argument that self-commendation is worthless and only the one 'whom the Lord commends' is approved (10:18; cf. 10:12). The shared self-praise/another-praises antithesis gives strong volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 10:17 'He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord' is a direct quotation of Jeremiah 9:24 (LXX 9:23), abbreviating the prophet's contrast: not the wise, mighty, or rich, but the one who understands and knows the LORD. The verbatim agreement and Paul's repeated use (also 1 Cor 1:31) make this a secure citation.

echoes.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”
echoes.note: 'It isn't he who commends himself who is approved, but whom the Lord commends' rests on the principle that the Lord, not human self-assessment, is the true evaluator — the same divine-versus-human judgment of 1 Samuel 16:7. Coherence with the appearance/heart contrast already invoked in 10:7 reinforces the allusion across the chapter.

echoes.text: The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places. Yes, I have a good inheritance.
echoes.note: Paul's boasting only 'within the boundaries (the measuring-line/sphere) which God appointed to us' echoes the lot/portion language of 'the boundary lines have fallen for me in pleasant places.' The shared notion of a divinely allotted measure or sphere supports a faint echo, though the metaphor is common.
echoes.altSource: Deuteronomy 32:8 (God fixed the boundaries of the peoples)

echoes.text: As clouds and wind without rain, so is he who boasts of gifts deceptively.
echoes.note: 'Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give' parallels Paul's refusal to 'boast in other men's labors' or in work not his own (10:15-16). The shared censure of empty boasting in what one has not done gives thematic coherence, but the link is faint.

pericopes.text: I wish that you would bear with me in a little foolishness, but indeed you do bear with me. For I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy. For I married you to one husband, that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. For if he who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive, or a different “good news”, which you did not accept, you put up with that well enough. For I reckon that I am not at all behind the very best apostles. But though I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not unskilled in knowledge. No, in every way we have been revealed to you in all things.

echoes.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion. I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know Yahweh.
echoes.note: Paul's claim to have 'betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ' draws on the prophetic marriage of YHWH to Israel, where God betroths his people to himself in righteousness and faithfulness. Hosea's betrothal language supplies the covenant-marriage logic underwriting Paul's 'godly jealousy.' Volume and coherence are strong since the bride/jealous-husband motif governs the whole pericope.

echoes.text: for you shall worship no other god: for Yahweh, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.
echoes.note: 'I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy' invokes the divine attribute that YHWH names his very self ('a jealous God,' literally 'whose name is Jealous'). The jealousy is covenantal: it presupposes the marriage bond and forbids rival lovers, precisely Paul's worry about 'another Jesus.' The conceptual link is dense even without verbatim quotation.

echoes.text: Again Yahweh’s word came to me, saying, Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations; and say, Thus says the Lord Yahweh to Jerusalem: Your birth and your birth is of the land of the Canaanite; the Amorite was your father, and your mother was a Hittite.
