As for your birth, in the day you were born your navel was not cut, neither were you washed in water to cleanse you; you weren’t salted at all, nor swaddled at all. No eye pitied you, to do any of […]
echoes.note: The figure of God espousing a people and the demand for the bride's purity (and the betrayal that follows) is most fully narrated in Ezekiel's allegory of Jerusalem as YHWH's bride. Paul's anxiety that the virgin will be corrupted/seduced coheres with Ezekiel's adultery imagery. Volume is diffuse, so allusion rather than quotation.

echoes.text: For your Maker is your husband; Yahweh of Armies is his name: and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer; the God of the whole earth shall he be called.
echoes.note: 'Your Maker is your husband' is the clearest single-verse statement of the divine-marriage theme that Paul presupposes when he presents the church as betrothed to Christ. The echo strengthens the coherence of the bride imagery in the pericope, though Paul does not cite it. Recurrence of the motif across Isaiah supports availability.

echoes.text: For as a young man marries a virgin, so your sons shall marry you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
echoes.note: 'As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you' contributes to the eschatological-marriage backdrop of presenting a pure virgin. Volume is low and the wording is not echoed, but the motif is coherent with Paul's betrothal language. Marked low as one strand of a cluster.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: 'As the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted' explicitly names the Eden narrative, where the serpent is more 'crafty/subtle' than any beast and Eve confesses 'the serpent deceived me.' This is a near-quotation of Genesis 3:13 LXX (the verb for deceive) plus 3:1 (craftiness). Volume, coherence, and explicit naming make this the surest OT use in the chapter.

echoes.text: They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God. They have provoked me to anger with their vanities. I will move them to jealousy with those who are not a people. I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.
echoes.note: The Song of Moses links Israel's turning to a foreign god with provoking YHWH to jealousy; Paul's pairing of jealousy with the threat of 'another Jesus' and 'a different spirit' coheres with that covenant-jealousy logic. Volume is faint and the connection is thematic. Flagged low as supporting the jealousy cluster.

pericopes.text: Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself that you might be exalted, because I preached to you God’s Good News free of charge? I robbed other assemblies, taking wages from them that I might serve you. When I was present with you and was in need, I wasn’t a burden on anyone, for the brothers, when they came from Macedonia, supplied the measure of my need. In everything I kept myself from being burdensome to you, and I will continue to do so. As the truth of Christ is in me, no one will stop me from this boasting in the regions of Achaia. Why? Because I don’t love you? God knows.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Paul's refusal of self-commendation and insistence on a 'boasting' rightly grounded (preaching free of charge, love attested by God who 'knows') anticipates the chapter's larger reframing of boasting along the lines of Jeremiah's 'let him who boasts boast in this, that he knows the Lord.' Volume here is low; the motif crystallizes more clearly at v. 30. Marked contested.

pericopes.text: But what I do, that I will do, that I may cut off occasion from them that desire an occasion, that in which they boast, they may be found even as we. For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as Christ’s apostles. And no wonder, for even Satan masquerades as an angel of light. It is no great thing therefore if his servants also masquerade as servants of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: The 'deceitful workers' who masquerade and the figure of Satan disguising himself extend the Eden serpent's deception introduced in v. 3. The serpent who appears attractive while corrupting coheres with false apostles masquerading as ministers of righteousness. Recurrence of the serpent motif within the chapter strengthens the link.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: 'Satan masquerades as an angel of light' has its closest extant parallel in the Adam-and-Eve pseudepigrapha, where Satan transforms himself into the brightness/form of an angel to deceive Eve a second time. This Second-Temple tradition explains why Paul attaches the disguise-as-light motif specifically to the serpent/Eve material of v. 3. Availability is plausible for a learned Pharisee; volume is conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: The Satan who moves among the 'sons of God' and operates by accusation and testing supplies the canonical adversary figure Paul names. The notion of Satan as a deceptive agent licensed within the heavenly court loosely coheres, though Job lacks the 'angel of light' disguise. Volume is faint; flagged low and contested.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary.
echoes.note: Satan standing to accuse Joshua the high priest before the angel of the LORD contributes to the canonical portrait of the satan as adversary opposing God's true servants, which Paul reapplies to those opposing his ministry. The link is thematic, not verbal. Marked low/contested.

echoes.text: How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!”
echoes.note: The 'Day Star/shining one' fallen from heaven who aspired to angelic/divine status was, in later reading, fused with Satan and supplies a figural backdrop for 'an angel of light.' Paul need not intend Isaiah directly, but the shining-but-false image coheres figurally. Availability of the fused tradition is Second-Temple-plausible; flagged low and contested.

pericopes.text: I say again, let no one think me foolish. But if so, yet receive me as foolish, that I also may boast a little. That which I speak, I don’t speak according to the Lord, but as in foolishness, in this confidence of boasting. Seeing that many boast after the flesh, I will also boast. For you bear with the foolish gladly, being wise. For you bear with a man, if he brings you into bondage, if he devours you, if he takes you captive, if he exalts himself, if he strikes you on the face. I speak by way of disparagement, as though we had been weak. Yet however any is bold (I speak in foolishness), I am bold also.

echoes.text: Don’t answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also be like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.
echoes.note: Paul's reluctant adoption of the fool's role ('receive me as foolish, that I also may boast a little'; 'answering' opponents on their own terms) plays on wisdom's paradox of whether to answer a fool according to his folly. The interplay of speaking-as-a-fool to expose folly coheres with Proverbs' aphorisms on fools and boasting. Volume is low; thematic only.

echoes.text: Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
echoes.note: 'Let another praise you, and not your own mouth' is the proverbial wisdom Paul transgresses self-consciously as he boasts 'after the flesh.' His apology for the foolish boast presupposes exactly this sapiential prohibition against self-praise. The echo is conceptual; flagged low and contested.

pericopes.text: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: 'Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I' appeals to the covenant promise of Abraham's 'seed,' the pedigree of God's elect people. The Abrahamic offspring formula is the foundation of the Hebrew/Israelite identity Paul claims. Volume rests on the loaded covenant term 'seed' rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”
echoes.note: The promise that Abraham's offspring would be innumerable underwrites the privileged status Paul invokes by naming himself 'seed of Abraham.' The verse is the classic charter of the lineage to which the opponents and Paul both lay claim. Coherence is high; verbal volume modest.

echoes.text: He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
echoes.note: 'Israelites' derives identity from Jacob's renaming as Israel, the eponymous ancestor of the covenant people Paul claims membership in. The link is etymological/identitarian rather than a textual citation. Marked low.

pericopes.text: Are they servants of Christ? (I speak as one beside himself) I am more so; in labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes above measure, in deaths often. Five times from the Jews I received forty stripes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck. I have been a night and a day in the deep. I have been in travels often, perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils from my countrymen, perils from the Gentiles, perils in the city, perils in the wilderness, perils in the sea, perils among false brothers; in labor and travail, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, and in cold and nakedness. Besides those things that are outside, there is that which presses on me daily, anxiety for all the assemblies. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I don’t burn with indignation?

echoes.text: If there is a controversy between men, and they come to judgment, and the judges judge them; then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked. It shall be, if the wicked man is worthy to be beaten, that the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face, according to his wickedness, by number. He may sentence him to no more than forty stripes. He shall not give more; lest, if he should give more, and beat him more than […]
echoes.note: 'Five times I received forty stripes minus one' presupposes the Torah's limit of forty lashes on a guilty man, with the synagogue practice of stopping at thirty-nine to avoid exceeding the law. The 'forty minus one' is unintelligible apart from this statute. Volume is high through the precise legal number even without quotation.

echoes.text: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but Yahweh delivers him out of them all.
echoes.note: 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all' frames Paul's catalog of sufferings as the lot of the righteous sufferer whom God preserves. The peristasis list reads as an enactment of this psalmic maxim, coherent with Paul's boast 'in weakness.' Volume is thematic.

echoes.text: therefore you will serve your enemies whom Yahweh sends against you, in hunger, in thirst, in nakedness, and in lack of all things. He will put an iron yoke on your neck, until he has destroyed you.
echoes.note: The covenant-curse list of serving 'in hunger, thirst, nakedness, and want of all things' supplies the lexical cluster behind Paul's 'hunger and thirst... cold and nakedness.' Paul ironically wears the curse-catalog as apostolic credential. Volume is low and the wording is common to affliction lists; flagged contested.

echoes.text: Now Pashhur, the son of Immer the priest, who was chief officer in Yahweh’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things. Then Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet, and put him in the stocks that were in the upper gate of Benjamin, which was in Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: The beating and imprisonment of the persecuted prophet Jeremiah typifies the suffering true messenger over against false prophets, the very contrast Paul presses against the 'super-apostles.' The link is figural, conforming Paul to the prophetic sufferer rather than citing a text. Marked low and contested.

echoes.text: Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck! I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold. I have come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
echoes.note: 'A night and a day in the deep,' perils of waters and being engulfed, resonate with the lament psalmist sinking in deep waters where the floods overwhelm him, a classic image of the righteous sufferer's distress. Volume is faint and the danger is literal for Paul, so flagged low and contested.

pericopes.text: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness. The God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, he who is blessed forever more, knows that I don’t lie. In Damascus the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes desiring to arrest me. Through a window I was let down in a basket by the wall, and escaped his hands.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness' inverts ordinary boasting along the lines of Jeremiah's oracle that the wise, mighty, and rich must not boast in their strength but only in knowing the LORD. Paul's recurring 'boast in the Lord' motif (cf. 10:17) makes this the controlling subtext for his weakness-boast. Coherence is strong across the letter.

echoes.text: Then she let them down by a cord through the window; for her house was on the side of the wall, and she lived on the wall.
echoes.note: The escape from Damascus, 'let down in a basket through a window by the wall,' replays Rahab lowering the spies by a rope through her window in the city wall. The shared escape-through-the-wall-window motif suggests Paul casts his flight in the idiom of the rescued/rescuing agent. Volume rests on the distinctive window-and-wall lowering.

echoes.text: So Michal let David down through the window. He went, fled, and escaped.
echoes.note: Michal lets David down through a window so he escapes the king who seeks his life, a close structural parallel to Paul evading King Aretas's governor. The persecuted-servant-lowered-through-a-window motif coheres, though Paul does not cite it. Offered as an alternative/companion source to the Rahab episode; flagged low.

echoes.text: Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.
echoes.note: 'The God and Father... who is blessed forever more' follows the berakah pattern of the psalter's doxologies ('Blessed be the LORD... forever and ever, Amen'). Paul's eulogy formula is liturgically shaped by such blessings. Volume is formulaic and low; flagged contested.

pericopes.text: It is doubtless not profitable for me to boast. For I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ, fourteen years ago (whether in the body, I don’t know, or whether out of the body, I don’t know; God knows), such a one caught up into the third heaven. I know such a man (whether in the body, or outside of the body, I don’t know; God knows), how he was caught up into Paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses. For if I would desire to boast, I will not be foolish; for I will speak the truth. But I refrain, so that no man may think more of me than that which he sees in me, or hears from me.

echoes.text: Now in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth of the month, as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.
echoes.note: Paul opens his account of ascent with the rubric 'visions and revelations of the Lord,' echoing the prophetic-apocalyptic technical language for throne and merkabah experience inaugurated by Ezekiel's 'I saw visions of God' (Ezek 1:1). The recurrence of such opening formulae across Ezekiel and Daniel makes this the native idiom Paul reworks; coherence is high since the whole pericope is a heavenly vision.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The apocalyptic 'visions' frame and the motif of being shown heavenly realities draw on Danielic seer-vision conventions, where Daniel beholds the divine throne 'in the visions of the night.' Faint and generic; flagged because Paul's vocabulary of revelation belongs to the Danielic apocalyptic stream that was available in the Second-Temple period.

echoes.text: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.
echoes.note: Paul says the man was 'caught up into Paradise' (paradeisos), the LXX word for the garden 'God planted in Eden.' The localization of Paradise in the highest heaven is a Second-Temple development from the Eden narrative; volume is moderate because the loaded term Paradise is a direct lexical link to the Genesis garden as rendered by the LXX.

echoes.text: You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone adorned you: ruby, topaz, emerald, chrysolite, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and beryl. Gold work of tambourines and of pipes was in you. In the day that you were created they were prepared.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's oracle places a figure 'in Eden, the garden of God,' fusing Eden with a glorious cosmic-mountain sanctuary, a trajectory that feeds the heavenly-Paradise of Paul's account. Coherence is strong because Ezekiel already relocates Eden into visionary, throne-adjacent space, the very move Paul presupposes when he equates the third heaven with Paradise.

echoes.text: He stretched out the form of a hand, and took me by a lock of my head; and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and the sky, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the gate of the inner court that looks toward the north; where there was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.
echoes.note: Paul's repeated uncertainty 'whether in the body or out of the body' and the verb 'caught up' recall prophetic rapture, as when the spirit 'lifted me up between earth and heaven' and brought Ezekiel in visions to Jerusalem. Faint but coherent: the motif of bodily-or-spiritual transport in vision is a prophetic precedent Paul reflexively invokes.

echoes.text: He said, “Go out, and stand on the mountain before Yahweh.” Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake.
echoes.note: The 'unspeakable words which it is not lawful to utter' loosely participates in the OT topos of an ineffable divine encounter, as at Horeb where the LORD passes by in a silence beyond the wind, earthquake, and fire. Very faint and contested; offered only because the apophatic restraint around theophany has OT roots, though Paul's secrecy is closer to apocalyptic sealing conventions.

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: The notion that what was heard 'is not lawful for a man to utter' resonates with the Sinai principle that direct apprehension of God's glory exceeds human bearing ('no man shall see me and live'). Faint; flagged because the unspeakable/unbearable quality of the highest revelation traces to the Mosaic theophany tradition Paul elsewhere engages closely (2 Cor 3).

pericopes.text: By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, that I should not be exalted excessively. Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me. He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me. Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.

echoes.text: “But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, then those you let remain of them will be as pricks in your eyes and as thorns in your sides, and they will harass you in the land in which you dwell.
echoes.note: The 'thorn in the flesh' draws on the LXX idiom for a persistent God-permitted affliction, where unexpelled inhabitants become 'thorns in your sides.' Volume and coherence are good: the metaphor of a thorn/goad lodged in the body as an ongoing scourge is precisely the OT figure Paul reworks into a personal torment.

echoes.text: There shall be no more a pricking brier to the house of Israel, nor a hurting thorn of any that are around them, that scorned them; and they shall know that I am the Lord Yahweh.
echoes.note: Ezekiel promises Israel relief from 'a pricking brier and a grieving thorn' from hostile neighbors, the same skolops/thorn imagery for a chronic harassment. The recurrence of this exact figure (Num, Josh, Ezek) for a divinely-tolerated irritant strengthens the case that Paul's 'thorn' is biblical metaphor, not merely medical.

echoes.text: know for a certainty that Yahweh your God will no longer drive these nations from out of your sight; but they shall be a snare and a trap to you, a scourge in your sides, and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good land which Yahweh your God has given you.
echoes.note: Joshua warns that the remaining nations will be 'scourges in your sides and thorns in your eyes,' pairing thorn with scourge exactly as Paul pairs his thorn with a tormenting 'messenger of Satan.' The combined thorn-and-scourge motif, recurring across the conquest texts, gives strong intertextual coherence to Paul's affliction language.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life.” So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
echoes.note: Paul's 'messenger of Satan to torment me' closely mirrors the prologue of Job, where the LORD permits the Satan to strike Job's flesh with sore boils. The structural parallel is strong: a faithful servant afflicted in the body by Satan under divine permission for a higher purpose, which frames Paul's theodicy of the thorn.

echoes.text: But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.
echoes.note: Paul's resolve to 'take pleasure in weaknesses... for Christ's sake' and to receive affliction without rebellion echoes Job's acceptance, 'shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?' Coherence is high because both texts make Satanic bodily affliction the arena of tested faithfulness rather than divine abandonment.

echoes.text: He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.
echoes.note: The divine word 'my power is made perfect in weakness' and 'when I am weak, then am I strong' enact Isaiah's promise that God 'gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength.' Volume is moderate but thematic coherence is strong: strength supplied precisely at the point of human exhaustion is Isaiah's consolation reapplied to apostolic suffering.

echoes.text: But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.
echoes.note: Paul's paradox that weakness is the condition of renewed power restates Isaiah's 'they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength.' Recurrence within the same Isaianic passage (40:29-31) and Paul's documented dependence on Isaiah in 2 Corinthians strengthen the link beyond a generic strength-theme.

echoes.text: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The principle that God's work advances through human weakness rather than human force recalls Zechariah's oracle, 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.' Coherence is strong: both deny that strength is the basis of God's accomplishment, locating efficacy in divine power, though Paul's wording is his own.

echoes.text: My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
echoes.note: Paul's confession that grace suffices when his own flesh fails echoes the psalmist's 'My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart.' The shared move from bodily failure to God as one's sustaining strength gives good thematic coherence to the grace-in-weakness motif.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
echoes.note: The promise that grace is sufficient and Christ's power rests on the weak loosely reflects the psalmic conviction that 'the LORD is near to those of a broken heart.' Faint and generic; included because Paul's grace-to-the-afflicted theology participates in the psalter's nearness-to-the-lowly tradition.

echoes.text: Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the tabernacle.
echoes.note: The phrase that 'the power of Christ may rest on me' (lit. 'tabernacle/dwell upon me,' episkenoo) faintly evokes the glory that 'filled the tabernacle' and overshadowed it at its consecration. Faint but offered because Paul's verb is cognate to tabernacle/skene, suggesting the indwelling Shekinah-glory now resting on the apostle's weak body.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The 'power of Christ' resting upon the apostle distantly echoes the Spirit of the LORD that 'shall rest upon' the messianic shoot. Faint; flagged because the resting of divine power/Spirit upon a chosen agent is an Isaianic figure, here transferred from Messiah to the one who bears Christ's power in weakness.

pericopes.text: I have become foolish in boasting. You compelled me, for I ought to have been commended by you, for in nothing was I inferior to the very best apostles, though I am nothing. Truly the signs of an apostle were worked among you in all patience, in signs and wonders and mighty works. For what is there in which you were made inferior to the rest of the assemblies, unless it is that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong.

echoes.text: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: Paul appeals to 'signs and wonders and mighty works' as the credentials of an apostle, using the fixed OT formula for God's authenticating acts, as when the LORD multiplied 'my signs and my wonders' in Egypt. Faint but coherent: the sign-and-wonder pairing is the Deuteronomistic vocabulary of divine accreditation that Paul transfers to apostolic ministry.

echoes.text: Or has God tried to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, by war, by a mighty hand, by an outstretched arm, and by great terrors, according to all that Yahweh your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?
echoes.note: The triad 'signs and wonders and mighty works' echoes Deuteronomy's recital of how God took Israel 'by signs, and by wonders... and by a mighty hand.' Recurrence of this credal formula across Deuteronomy strengthens the case that Paul deliberately borrows the language of God's saving demonstrations to mark genuine apostleship.

pericopes.text: Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you; for I seek not your possessions, but you. For the children ought not to save up for the parents, but the parents for the children. I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more abundantly, am I loved the less? But be it so, I did not myself burden you. But, being crafty, I caught you with deception. Did I take advantage of you by anyone of them whom I have sent to you? I exhorted Titus, and I sent the brother with him. Did Titus take any advantage of you? Didn’t we walk in the same spirit? Didn’t we walk in the same steps?

echoes.text: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the wealth of the sinner is stored for the righteous.
echoes.note: Paul's maxim 'the parents should save up for the children, not the children for the parents' inverts and applies the proverbial principle that 'a good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children.' Coherence is good because Paul reasons from the accepted wisdom convention of parental provision to justify his refusal to burden his spiritual children.

echoes.text: House and riches are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife is from Yahweh.
echoes.note: The assumption that fathers lay up substance for their offspring also reflects 'house and riches are an inheritance from fathers.' Faint and overlapping with Prov 13:22; included to register the broader wisdom topos of inherited parental provision that undergirds Paul's analogy.

pericopes.text: Again, do you think that we are excusing ourselves to you? In the sight of God we speak in Christ. But all things, beloved, are for your edifying. For I am afraid that by any means, when I come, I might find you not the way I want to, and that I might be found by you as you don’t desire; that by any means there would be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, factions, slander, whisperings, proud thoughts, riots; that again when I come my God would humble me before you, and I would mourn for many of those who have sinned before now, and not repented of the uncleanness and sexual immorality and lustfulness which they committed.

echoes.text: Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceit: one speaks peaceably to his neighbor with his mouth, but in his heart he lays wait for him.
echoes.note: Paul's feared catalog of communal sins (strife, jealousy, anger, slander, whisperings) echoes the prophetic indictments of Israel's social corruption, as in Jeremiah's complaint that the tongue 'speaks deceit... one speaks peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth, but in his heart he lays his wait.' Faint and diffuse, but coherent with the prophetic tradition of cataloguing the sins that fracture the covenant community.

echoes.text: There are six things which Yahweh hates; yes, seven which are an abomination to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood; a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that are swift in running to mischief, a false witness who utters lies, and he who sows discord among brothers.
echoes.note: Paul's vice-list culminating in one who 'sows discord' parallels the wisdom catalog of things the LORD hates, which ends with 'one who sows discord among brothers' and includes a lying tongue and a false witness. The shared form of an enumerated list of community-destroying sins gives modest coherence, though Paul's specific terms are his own.

echoes.text: I also walked contrary to them, and brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled, and they then accept the punishment of their iniquity;
echoes.note: Paul's fear that God 'would humble me before you' and that he must mourn over the unrepentant draws on the covenantal pattern wherein the people's 'uncircumcised heart' is humbled until they repent. Faint; flagged because the humbling-then-mourning-over-sin sequence reflects the Levitical/Deuteronomic logic of covenant discipline.

echoes.text: Thus will I cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to do after your lewdness.
echoes.note: Paul's lament over 'the uncleanness and sexual immorality and lustfulness' of the unrepentant echoes Ezekiel's prophetic language of Israel's lewdness and uncleanness for which the people must be judged and turned. Faint and thematic; included because Paul's grief over sexual impurity in the congregation belongs to the prophetic idiom of denouncing covenantal 'uncleanness.'

pericopes.text: This is the third time I am coming to you. “At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.” I have said beforehand, and I do say beforehand, as when I was present the second time, so now, being absent, I write to those who have sinned before now, and to all the rest, that, if I come again, I will not spare; seeing that you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me; who toward you is not weak, but is powerful in you. For he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we will live with him through the power of God toward you.

echoes.text: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sins. At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall a matter be established.
echoes.note: Paul cites the two-or-three-witnesses rule verbatim ('At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established'), a direct LXX-form quotation governing judicial proof. Volume is maximal: explicit citation formula and near-verbatim wording. Coherence is strong since Paul frames his three visits as the requisite testimony before disciplinary action.

echoes.text: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, he who is to die shall be put to death. At the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.
echoes.note: The same Deuteronomic two-or-three-witnesses principle appears here in a capital-case context, part of the legal tradition Paul invokes. The wording overlaps with Deut 19:15, the primary source, so this is a parallel attestation of the rule rather than the citation's lemma. Recurrence within the Torah strengthens the availability of the witness-tradition.

echoes.text: “‘Whoever kills any person, the murderer shall be slain at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against any person that he die.
echoes.note: Numbers also codifies that a person shall be put to death only on the testimony of witnesses, reinforcing the multi-witness legal tradition Paul deploys. It is a secondary attestation alongside Deut 17:6 rather than the quoted text. The cluster shows the rule's standing as established Torah jurisprudence.

echoes.text: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed? For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and […]
echoes.note: Christ 'crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God' echoes the Servant who is afflicted and humbled yet exalted and vindicated by God. Volume is faint and no verbal citation occurs, so the link rests on the conceptual coherence of suffering-then-power. Contested because the weakness/power dialectic is broadly Pauline and not demonstrably keyed to Isaiah here.

pericopes.text: Test your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves. Or don’t you know as to your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you are disqualified. But I hope that you will know that we aren’t disqualified. Now I pray to God that you do no evil; not that we may appear approved, but that you may do that which is honorable, though we are as reprobate. For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong. And this we also pray for, even your perfecting. For this cause I write these things while absent, that I may not deal sharply when present, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for building up, and not for tearing down.

echoes.text: Examine me, Yahweh, and prove me. Try my heart and my mind.
echoes.note: Paul's 'Test your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves' resonates with the psalmist's 'Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; test my heart and my mind.' Volume is moderate through shared testing/proving vocabulary in the self-scrutiny tradition. Coherence is high since both concern verifying genuine standing before God.

echoes.text: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
echoes.note: The summons to be searched and tested to see whether any wicked way is present parallels Paul's call to self-examination 'whether you are in the faith.' The introspective testing tradition supplies the conceptual frame for Paul's appeal. No verbal quotation, so this is an allusion within a recurrent biblical motif.

echoes.text: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD' supplies a corporate self-examination motif close to Paul's command to test oneself. Volume is faint with no shared diction in Greek, so the echo is thematic. Coherence is supported by the repentance/restoration aim of the surrounding verses (perfecting, doing no evil).

echoes.text: The refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, but Yahweh tests the hearts.
echoes.note: 'The refining pot is for silver... but the LORD tests the hearts' belongs to the wisdom tradition of divine testing that informs Paul's language of approval and being 'reprobate/disqualified' (adokimos). The link is conceptual rather than verbal and competes with the Psalms as a closer source. Marked contested for its faintness.

pericopes.text: Finally, brothers, rejoice. Be perfected, be comforted, be of the same mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

echoes.text: Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: 'Live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you' echoes the Aaronic benediction's 'the LORD... give you peace,' the foundational peace-blessing of Israel. Volume is moderate via the shared peace-and-presence formula closing the letter. Coherence is strong since Paul is pronouncing a farewell blessing, the benediction's native function.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The full priestly blessing (grace/favor, the LORD's face, peace) stands behind Paul's closing of peace and divine presence and anticipates the triune benediction in v.14. The threefold structure of grace, love, and fellowship loosely mirrors the threefold Aaronic form. Marked allusion rather than quotation given the absence of verbatim wording.

echoes.text: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
echoes.note: The divine title 'the God of love and peace' faintly recalls covenantal peace-name traditions such as Gideon's altar 'The LORD is Peace' (YHWH-shalom). The connection is purely thematic with no verbal overlap, so it is a faint echo. Contested and secondary to the Aaronic blessing as the operative source.

pericopes.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all. Amen.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The closing triune benediction ('the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit') functions as Paul's Christianized Aaronic blessing, its threefold grace/presence/peace structure refracted into a threefold divine formula. Volume rests on the shared benedictory genre and triadic shape rather than diction. Coherence is high: a letter-closing priestly-style blessing invoking grace and the divine presence 'with you all.'

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: 'The love of God' draws on the covenant self-revelation of the LORD as abounding in steadfast love (hesed), the wellspring of Israel's confidence in divine favor. The echo is conceptual, supplying the OT substrate for 'love of God,' with no verbal citation. Contested because 'love of God' is a generic Pauline phrase not demonstrably keyed to this text.
